name: Half Fast
beta: Mix of sport bolts and trad placements. South-facing provides good sun exposure. Straightforward climbing with consistent protection.
overview: A solid moderate route with good flow and continuous climbing on slab and crack. Excellent for building confidence.

current.approach: Take US-2 east from Seattle/Everett over Stevens Pass, then drop onto the old Stevens Pass Highway (now Tye Rd), which heads toward the Iron Horse Trailhead and the Wellington townsite; park in the pullout just uphill of a double hairpin turn roughly 1.4 miles from US-2. From there, the on-foot approach follows only faint boot-path traces through open old-growth forest, generally trending uphill and left across a drainage to reach the base of the crag. Expect about 1,000 feet of elevation gain and 45-60 minutes of hiking, with route-finding skills helpful since the tread is intermittent.
current.descent: Rappel 50 feet from anchors to ground.
current.detailed_rack: Standard sport rack with 10-12 quickdraws, wired stoppers (sizes 1-4), medium nuts (sizes 1-3), 60m rope, locking carabiners.
rack: 10-12 quickdraws
Wired stoppers (sizes 1-4)
Nuts (sizes 1-3)
60m dynamic rope
current.pro_needs: Lead climber comfortable on 5.8+ with mixed protection (bolts and natural gear). Solid footwork and crack skills.

name: Helmet Butte Standard Route
beta: Helmet Butte is normally climbed as part of a Buck Creek Pass backpacking trip rather than a car-to-car day climb, given the ~17.6-mile round-trip approach. From a point at 5,600 ft on the Buck Creek Pass Trail ('Waypoint 86'), the recommended line turns off-trail toward Pass No Pass on a well-defined but braiding boot path, gains a notch around 7,200 ft below the summit block, then finishes with a short, low-exposure Class 3 scramble on solid rock, aiming for the block's south (left) side for the easiest line. An alternate line continues past the trail junction to Buck Creek Pass itself, then climbs steep grass and heather slopes to the west side of the summit block before the same short scramble - this option is likely hazardous when wet.
overview: A non-technical but exposed Class 3 scramble to a well-defined granodiorite summit block, reached via a long approach up the Buck Creek Pass Trail and then an off-trail push through meadows above Pass No Pass (or, alternately, up steep grass/heather from Buck Creek Pass).

current.approach: From Coles Corner on US-2 (about 20 miles east of Stevens Pass), take WA-207 north 4.4 miles, turn right onto Chiwawa Loop Road for 1.3 miles, then left onto Chiwawa River Road (Forest Road 6200) and follow it roughly 23 miles to its end at the Trinity / Buck Creek Pass Trailhead (about 2,772-2,800 ft). Important: storm damage has closed FR 6200 to vehicles beyond Atkinson Flat Campground, cutting off drive-in access to Trinity, and wildfire closures have also shut the road and the Buck Creek Trail - confirm current status with the Wenatchee River Ranger District before relying on this approach. From the trailhead, hike the Buck Creek Trail #1513 (signed Buck Creek Pass Trail #789 on Forest Service pages), climbing steadily through forest and along Buck Creek roughly 8.8 miles to about 5,600 ft, where the standard line breaks off-trail to the right toward Pass No Pass.
approach_variant_names: Buck Creek Trail to Pass No Pass
Buck Creek Pass and the grass slopes
current.descent: From the summit, downclimb the short Class 3 block on its south side, descend the grassy slopes back through the Pass No Pass notch (or, if the west-side variant was used, back down the steep grass/heather to Buck Creek Pass), rejoin the maintained Buck Creek Pass Trail at about 5,600 ft, and follow it roughly 8.8 miles back down to the Trinity Trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rock or ice gear is needed - this is a hiking/scrambling route.
current.pro_needs: None - the Class 3 summit block is unroped scrambling on generally solid rock with a short, low-exposure crux.
bivy: Buck Creek Pass and the High Pass camps

name: Henpecked
beta: A simple, blocky line to a bolted anchor.
overview: Sport climb on Minidike.

current.approach: The Dikes sit in the Umatilla National Forest's Walla Walla Ranger District, in the East Fork Touchet River valley near Ski Bluewood, southeast Washington — not near the Snake River. Access is via North Touchet Road out of Dayton, WA, paved for roughly the first 15-16 miles before becoming gravel Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary; the road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter, but snow on the crags and approach slopes keeps the climbing season to roughly May-October, sometimes from April. Approaches are very short and roadside: the south Megadike is reached by parking near a bridge 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and scrambling directly up the steep hillside above the bridge abutment, while Weeping Wall and Joe's Rock are similar short pullout-to-cliff scrambles at 1.1 and 2.0 miles past the same trailhead respectively. The area is lightly visited and faint-trailed, and the basalt is notably loose/fractured, requiring routine loose-rock cleaning. For the Minidike, pull off 1.5 miles beyond the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead, on the left (SE) side of the road immediately after the bridge over the river. Cross the road, scramble down the bridge abutment, and follow a trail downstream on the NW side.
current.descent: Lower from the anchor on a single strand.
current.detailed_rack: Bolted with anchors at top; standard sport rack for a short pitch.
current.pro_needs: Fully bolted.
current.rope_note: Single-pitch bolted sport route at Minidike (The Dikes, WA). Minidike routes are shorter than Megadike; 60m is sufficient.

name: Standard Scramble
beta: From the Rachel Lake trailhead, follow the maintained Rachel Lake Trail for roughly 2 miles to the first avalanche-chute clearing. A boot path for Hibox leaves the main trail here (or at the second chute crossing) and climbs steeply but stays class 2 through timber to near treeline. Above the trees, go right around the first band of cliffs, then left around a rock outcrop, continue through more timber to a second cliff band, and take the gully on the right to gain the upper mountain. From there head right (east) along the south side of the summit rocks to a gully on the east side, which is climbed with a bit of class 3 near the top to reach the summit. Route-finding is the main challenge; there is no continuous trail above the boot path.
overview: Hibox Mountain (6,548 ft) is the high point of Box Ridge, a rugged sub-ridge of the Alpine Lakes Wilderness about 5 miles east of Snoqualmie Pass, rising above the popular Rachel Lake basin. It's one of the most-climbed scrambles near I-90, combining an easy trail approach with a steep, loose Class 2-3 boot path up Box Ridge and a short, exposed Class 3 summit block. Summit views take in Rampart Ridge, Alta Mountain, Three Queens, Mount Thompson, Rachel Lake, and the Stuart Range.

current.approach: Start at the Rachel Lake Trailhead (Trail #1313, elev. ~2,800 ft) at the end of Box Canyon Road/FR-4930. Follow the Rachel Lake Trail as it climbs gently through forest along the Box Canyon Creek drainage — the grade is easy and well-graded here, mostly Class 1 hiking. At roughly 2–2.2 miles and about 450–500 ft of gain (~3,300 ft elevation), the trail crosses a brushy avalanche-path clearing where Hibox's summit block comes into view on the ridge to the northeast; this clearing is the key landmark. Just past it (some parties note it's after the second such clearing), watch on the right/climber's-right side of the trail for an unmarked but well-established boot path (the 'Hibox climbers' path') leaving the maintained trail and heading northeast/uphill into the forest — it's easy to walk past if you're not looking for it. From here the character changes completely: the bootpath climbs steeply (mostly Class 2, with fallen timber to step over) before breaking out of the trees near a band of cliffs around 5,300 ft. Stay right of this first rock band, then work left around a rock outcrop, continuing through patchy timber to a second, higher cliff band; a gully on the right provides passage through it. Above this the trail opens into a large sloping subalpine meadow (wildflowers in season) that funnels into a loose talus/scree slope — this is the most tedious and slip-prone section of the route, so careful foot placement matters more than pace. A thready boot path threads up through the talus to the south side of the summit block. There is no reliable water past the lower forest/creek section, so carry what you need from the car or treat water low on the mountain. The route-finding through the two cliff bands and the avalanche-path junction low on the trail are the two spots parties most often go astray; a GPS track or recent trip report beta is worth having.
approach_variant_names: Rachel Lake Trail to the avalanche clearing, then the Hibox climbers' path over two cliff bands
current.descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line rather than glissading the scree, which is loose and eroded. From the summit, downclimb the short exposed notch/cleft back to the south side of the summit block (good rock, low exposure, easy Class 3 moves), then pick your way back down through the loose talus/scree field to the sloping meadow. Some parties descend via a slightly different line on the east side of the summit block/east ridge before rejoining the ascent boot path lower down — functionally the same route, just avoid cutting new paths through the scree to limit erosion. Continue down through the two cliff bands (reversing right/left as on the way up) and back into the timber, staying alert for the boot path's exit point onto the maintained Rachel Lake Trail near the ~3,300 ft avalanche clearing — it's easy to miss in the trees when descending. Once back on Rachel Lake Trail #1313, it's an easy, well-graded 2+ miles back to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb route with no rappelling required — the summit block's only technical move is a short, low-exposure Class 3 downclimb, not a rappel. Watch the weather: afternoon thunderstorms are common in this range and parties often report hurrying off the loose upper slopes ahead of incoming storms.
current.detailed_rack: No real rack; a short rope and a sling optional for the exposed summit block.
current.pro_needs: Minimal.

name: Standard Route
beta: First ascensionists Cooper, Denny, and the Fireys found the peak unpromising from either flanking notch, then located a class-4 route by following a ledge onto the north face that wasn't visible from below. The line is mostly scrambling with short steeper steps; conditions and difficulty vary considerably with season and snow coverage in the approach gully.
overview: Himmelhorn (originally Himmelgeisterhorn, "Horn of the Sky Spirit") is one of the most sought-after summits of the Southern Pickets, sitting on the crest between Ottohorn/Frenzel Spitz to the west and Twin Needles/Mount Terror to the east, with the small Mustard Glacier draped on its north side. It was first climbed September 8, 1961 by Ed Cooper, Glen Denny, Joan Firey, Joe Firey, and George Whitmore, who approached via the west notch (the Himmel-Otto col) and found a class 4 line up a ledge system onto the north/northwest face — no summit cairn was found, confirming the true first ascent. The peak remains a serious objective less for sustained technical difficulty than for its position deep in one of the most remote, brush-choked corners of North Cascades National Park; parties commonly link it with neighboring Ottohorn and/or Frenzel Spitz from a shared Crescent Creek Basin camp. Other established lines on the peak include the classic Wild Hair Crack (5.7, west face, Kroeker/Roper/Wild, 1981) and the harder South Face "Stonehenge" (5.10-, 8 pitches, Schilling/Halder, 2015).

current.approach: From the Goodell Creek Campground/Trailhead on SR 20 just west of Newhalem (~600 ft), follow the old decommissioned logging roadbed along the true left (south) side of Goodell Creek. This grassy/gravel roadbed is flat and easy hiking for roughly 4 to 4.5 miles, gaining only a few hundred feet to about 1,700-1,800 ft. Watch on the right for a cairn/stone marker (climbers call it the 'stone arrow') at the end of the roadbed - this marks the unsigned but well-boot-beaten climbers' path that leaves the creek bottom and switchbacks steeply up into old-growth forest toward Stump Hollow and Terror Creek Basin. This user trail is steep, root-and-duff footing, and brushy in spots (slide alder, devil's club low down) but stays reasonably distinct with flagging/cairns in the upper sections; there is no reliable water between the roadbed's end and treeline, so top off at Goodell Creek. Around 5,000-5,600 ft the forest opens into Stump Hollow, a slabby heather-and-snowfield basin wedged between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block - a scenic, easier-angle respite after the timber grind. From Stump Hollow, rising-traverse on meadow, slab, and (early/mid-season) snow to a broad saddle on the Barrier ridge at roughly 6,200 ft. Cross the Barrier itself by one of two options: a lower crossing on a loose, exposed ledge system at the toe of the Terror Glacier, or a higher crossing over moat terrain and steep choss just below Mt. Degenhardt; either takes under an hour but involves loose rock and some exposure, so care with rockfall onto any party below is essential. Descend the far side into Crescent Creek Basin (good bivy sites and reliable running water, roughly below Mt. Terror) - this is the standard camp for Himmelhorn objectives. From camp, ascend the narrow gully leading to the Himmel-Otto col: in early season this is a straightforward snow climb with a bit of scrambling near the top; by late season the gully turns to icy hardpack with choss-filled moats along the rock margins, and an overhanging boulder near the col often forces a loose, exposed class 3-4 bypass on the left (climber's) side. From the col, the standard route continues up easier ground (scrambling to low 5th class) onto Himmelhorn's northwest flank to the 7,880 ft summit. Total approach distance to the summit and back runs on the order of 15-16 miles round trip with substantial elevation gain and loss, so most parties treat this as a 2-4 day trip with a basecamp in Crescent Creek Basin rather than a car-to-car push.
approach_variant_names: Goodell Creek and the stone arrow, Stump Hollow, the Barrier, and the Himmel-Otto col gully
current.descent: Descend by reversing the route: downclimb (with short rappels where the rock steepens or is wet/icy) from the summit back down to the Himmel-Otto col, then retrace the approach gully back down into Crescent Creek Basin. Early in the season this gully descent is a quick, straightforward snow glissade/plunge-step with minimal fuss; by late season, when the gully has melted out to icy hardpack and choss-filled moats, parties often find fixed or placed rap anchors in the moat sections more reliable than downclimbing loose rock next to hard snow/ice. From Crescent Creek Basin, reverse the entire approach: recross the Barrier (lower ledge or upper moat/choss option), drop back through Stump Hollow, and pick up the steep climbers' path back down through the timber to the old Goodell Creek roadbed and out to the trailhead. There are no bolted or fixed rappel stations on this route - any anchors encountered or built (slings around horns/blocks/chockstones) are natural, climber-placed gear anchors typical of this remote, seldom-visited range, so carry a small rack of slings/cord and a couple of rappel-rated tat-worthy items in case the moat or upper gully requires a rappel to protect the loose, exposed terrain near the col. A single 60m rope is adequate for any rappels on this route (the terrain near the col is broken into short steps, not a sustained wall). Watch for rockfall in the gully and on the Barrier crossings, especially with parties above, and for the choss/loose-rock hazard around the overhanging boulder bypass near the col, which is exposed in both directions.
current.detailed_rack: A light alpine rack is typical for this class-IV/low-5th line: a small set of nuts and cams, a few slings/draws, and a lightweight rope for the short technical sections and any rappels off the col.
rack: Light alpine rack: small set of nuts and cams
A few slings/draws
Lightweight rope for short technical sections and rappels off the col
current.pro_needs: Protection needs are modest and intermittent — mostly natural gear placements on broken, blocky rock for short exposed sections rather than sustained crack climbing.
bivy: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
High bivouacs at the western end of the crest
current.rope_note: Remote alpine rock and scramble route in the Southern Pickets: a long off-trail approach and col gully, then class 4 to low fifth-class rock from the col. The descent reverses the route by downclimbing and short rappels. Bring extra tat; anchors are minimal in this range.

name: Stonehenge
beta: First climbed July 6, 2015 by Jason Schilling and Tim Halder, based out of a camp below the Chopping Block above Crescent Creek. The route climbs blocky ground low, a crux pitch 2 (5.10-) that leaves a dead-end dihedral and traverses left onto the face to a hand crack, moves through easier pitches, then tackles two more steep, run-out 5.8/5.10- faces higher on a distinct summit tower before an easy, loose finishing pitch. Rock quality was reported as predominantly solid to excellent higher on the face. Named after watching Spinal Tap's 'Stonehenge' scene at camp post-climb.
overview: An 8-pitch 5.10- line up Himmelhorn's previously-unclimbed south face, established in July 2015, finishing up a summit tower via steep, run-out faces separated by easier ground.

current.approach: From a high camp below the Chopping Block above Crescent Creek Basin, the party left at 4 a.m., reached the snow slope below the wall by 5 a.m., then climbed roughly 600 ft of easy rock ramps and ledges to a grassy col at the base of the wall where they racked up.
approach_variant_names: From a high camp below the Chopping Block, up the snow slope and 600 ft of ramps to the grassy col at the base of the wall
current.descent: From the top of the difficulties, a traverse reaches a notch on the ridge, and one easy but loose pitch leads from there up to the summit. No descent line or rappel count has been recorded for the way back down.
current.pro_needs: A standard alpine trad rack for 5.10 crack and face climbing; there is no more specific gear list.

name: Honeymoon Route
beta: A steep snow couloir climb on the mountain's northeast aspect, reported by climbers as a direct, sustained line taking roughly 3 hours from upper Royal Lake Basin to the top of the couloir in good snow conditions. It sees a narrow seasonal window — climbed successfully in both an early-summer trip report and at least one winter ascent — and functions as the technical/snow-climbing counterpart to the standard rock scramble.
overview: Also known as the Northeast Couloir or Northeast Chute, this is a steeper, more direct alternative to the standard scramble, climbing a prominent NE-facing snow couloir from upper Royal Basin straight to the upper mountain.

current.approach: From the Upper Dungeness/Royal Basin Trailhead (elev. ~2,500 ft), hike the Upper Dungeness River Trail roughly 7 miles with about 2,500 ft of gain to Royal Lake, then continue about a mile farther into Upper Royal Basin (~5,600 ft), a meadow-and-tarn basin ringed by Deception, Mystery, Fricaba, and Hal Foss Peak. From the upper basin, leave the trail and head southwest over the moraine to the big snow slope on the west edge of the northeast face. Climb it most of the way toward the low point of the Deception-Martin ridge, then break left into the steep side gully that gives the route its name; from its top, traverse left and climb a second snow-and-rock gully to the summit ridge. Allow roughly 3 hours from the upper basin to the top of the gully in good snow. A Northwest Forest Pass is needed at the trailhead and a wilderness permit is required for overnight stays. In early May water runs freely beside the trail up to roughly 5,700 ft, so there is no need to melt snow on the way in.
approach_variant_names: Royal Basin to the Northeast Couloir
current.descent: Climbers typically downclimb or glissade the couloir if snow conditions allow, or traverse to descend via the standard route's looser terrain; either way the exit funnels back through upper Royal Basin to Royal Lake and the maintained trail.
current.detailed_rack: Not a roped rock climb for most parties in normal conditions. A rope and glacier gear are not needed for the small glacier remnant traverse (no meaningful crevasse hazard reported), but a rope, a few slings, and light rock protection can be prudent for parties wanting to belay short class 3-4 sections or the Gilhooley Tower area in early/lean-snow conditions.
current.pro_needs: Standard steep-snow-climbing protection: ice axe and often a second tool, crampons, and a helmet; this is an unroped or occasionally short-roped snow climb rather than a pitched, protected route in the trip reports found.
current.rope_note: Direct snow-gully route: continuous ~45-degree snow climb to hard mud/loose Class 3 rock. No rope or other usual glacier gear is needed, but a helmet is essential because of loose rock.

name: Honeymoon Sweet
beta: A moderate single-pitch sport climb that angles slightly left near the top to a chain anchor at the top of the cliff; the first bolted line established in the Spire Gully area, put up by its namesake honeymooning first-ascent party.
overview: The original, historic sport route at the Spire Gully/Alpenkuhl crag — a moderate 50-foot single pitch.

current.approach: From the Washington Pass 'hairpin' turnout on SR-20 (~1 mile east of Washington Pass), park in a roadside pullout (no permit required). Follow the climbers' trail uphill toward Spire Gully; the Alpenkuhl wall is the sunny, south-facing side of the gully. Approach takes about 7 minutes (may be snow-covered in early season).
current.descent: Tops out at a chain anchor at the top of the cliff. Lower directly to the ground on a single rope; no walk-off or rappel is required.
current.pro_needs: Fully bolted, 5 bolts to a chain anchor.

name: Raven Ridge Traverse
beta: From the Libby Lake approach trail, climb a loose gully to gain Raven Ridge, then follow the ridge crest toward Hoodoo Peak. The first half of the ridge is easy class 2-3, but where it bends toward Hoodoo it steepens into sustained, exposed class 4 knife-edge scrambling. A roughly 10-ft overhanging step partway along requires either a solid 5.7 boulder-problem move or a short rappel to bypass; the final stretch to the Hoodoo summit eases back to class 2 boulders, with optional class 3-4 scrambling available along the ridge crest.
overview: A committing ridge traverse linking Raven Ridge to Hoodoo Peak via a loose approach gully and a narrow, increasingly knife-edged crest with one short 5.7 crux.

current.approach: Hike the trail toward Libby Lake, then leave the trail and climb a loose talus/scree gully to gain the crest of Raven Ridge; a helmet is worthwhile given loose rock in the gully.
current.descent: From Hoodoo's summit, downclimb the easy scree/talus slope on the peak's flank back to the approach trail near Libby Lake, avoiding a reversal of the exposed ridge crest.
current.pro_needs: No fixed protection reported; a short rope/sling is only used to rappel or protect the single 5.7 overhanging step on the ridge.

name: Standard Scramble
beta: Most parties approach via the trail toward Libby Lake in the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness, then leave the trail to climb scree and boulder slopes toward Hoodoo Peak's summit ridge; the final stretch is mostly class 2 boulder-hopping with occasional easy class 3 moves.
overview: Hoodoo Peak (8,475 ft) is a Methow Mountains summit — the easternmost sub-range of the North Cascades — within the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest's Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness, near the southern end of the range above Lake Chelan. It ranks among the higher summits on Washington's Bulger List (the state's 100 highest peaks) but is regarded as one of the easier Bulger objectives, a Class 2-3 boulder/talus scramble reached via the Libby Lake Trail. Its parent peak, Raven Ridge (8,590 ft), rises about 0.9 mi to the south and is a common (harder) add-on via a class 3-4 ridge traverse. The peak is especially popular in late September/early October, when the basin below Libby Lake and the approach slopes fill with golden larches.

current.approach: From the Libby Lake Trailhead (a.k.a. Libby Creek Trailhead, ~4,430 ft; no parking fee or pass required at this trailhead) at the end of Libby Creek Road, follow Libby Creek Trail No. 415 southwest into the Lake Chelan–Sawtooth Wilderness. The trail climbs gradually through mixed conifer forest and crosses several tributaries of Libby Creek on logs or hoppable rocks (trekking poles help); tread can be brushy/overgrown in the lower stretches. The first reliable water is a spring in the burn scar, and the ford of North Fork Libby Creek, about halfway to Libby Lake, has a campsite on the far bank. At about 4.5 miles you reach a decaying historic line cabin in a clearing — the key junction on this route: continuing straight/west climbs a final steep half-mile (~470 ft) to Libby Lake (7,740 ft), a common basecamp and especially scenic in larch season (late Sept–early Oct), while the right-hand fork is the climbers' route toward Hoodoo. The route does not go to Libby Lake: take the faint boot path to the right of the cabin into open forest, then pick a line up the boulder field and loose gully to the pass on the ridge south of the summit. Once off-trail there is no maintained tread and the boulder field has no single obvious line, so route-finding care is needed — this is the route's main hazard, especially in fog or flat light. From the ridge crest, turn north and follow it over a broad boulder field to the summit; the final stretch is continuous class 2 boulder-hopping with occasional class 3 moves, and loose rock is common, so test holds before weighting them. Snow can linger in the ascent gully and on the upper ridge into June, so carry an ice axe (crampons recommended) for May–June attempts.
approach_variant_names: Libby Creek Trail #415 to Libby Lake
current.descent: The standard descent is a straight reversal of the ascent: back down the summit boulder field to the pass south of the summit, down the entry gully and boulder field to the old cabin, and out Libby Creek Trail No. 415 to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/scramble descent with no rappelling required (rappels: 0) — no ropes, anchors, or technical gear are needed on the standard route. Some parties descend slightly skier's-left (east) of their ascent line through looser scree for a more direct, faster line off the boulder field, but this variation is steeper and looser underfoot, so it's a judgment call rather than the default. The main descent hazard is footing in the unstable talus/boulder field rather than exposure — most reported close calls on Hoodoo come from rolled ankles or shifting rock, not falls. Note that a connecting ridge traverse to neighboring Raven Ridge is a distinct, harder outing involving an exposed knife-edged 4th-class section and at least one short technical rappel/downclimb near a rock overhang — that beta belongs to the traverse route, not to this standard scramble.
current.pro_needs: Unroped class 2-3 scramble; no technical gear normally required.
bivy: Old cabin camp, Libby Creek trail
current.rope_note: Class 2 boulder scramble with reportedly minimal exposure; no rope used on the standard route.

name: Standard Route
beta: From Sahale Glacier Camp (or a Horseshoe Basin camp), cross into Horseshoe Basin, gain the base of a class 3 dike/gully system below Ripsaw Ridge, and follow it (with a short class 4 step) up to the ridge crest near the 'Lick of Flame' spire. From there a narrow ramp leads to the summit; it begins as 3rd-class terrain and turns into a short section of 5th-class (5.2) climbing in its final ~100 ft below the top. Rope up for this last section — most parties treat it as one roughly 100-ft pitch. Descend by a single rappel off a horn on the summit (backed by old fixed webbing) or downclimb the same dike/ramp system, then retrace the approach.
overview: Horseshoe Peak (8,480+ ft per the 1963 USGS Cascade Pass quad) is the high point of Ripsaw Ridge, a knife-edge arête connecting Boston Peak to Mt. Buckner, about a quarter-mile west of Buckner's summit, on the Skagit/Chelan county line deep in the Cascade Pass / Sahale Arm high country of North Cascades NP. With only ~80 ft of prominence it's really a subsidiary tower on the ridge rather than a standalone peak, but it made the Bulgers' Washington Top 100 list on the strength of its height and named status. It's rated an easy Grade II, 5.2 rock climb: mostly loose Class 3 scrambling with one short, exposed 5th-class step through a notch just below the true summit. Most parties combine it with Sahale Peak and/or Mt. Buckner in a single long day or overnight, since all three share the same Sahale Arm / Horseshoe Basin approach.

current.approach: From the Cascade Pass Trailhead (end of the Cascade River Road — gravel/washboard, high-clearance/AWD recommended), climb the well-graded Cascade Pass Trail switchbacks 3.7 mi and about 1,800 ft to the broad 5,400-ft saddle at Cascade Pass. Two standard lines converge on Horseshoe Peak from here, both eventually crossing loose, unmaintained terrain above the pass. Sahale Arm option: continue past the Cascade Pass junction onto the Sahale Arm Trail, climbing the open heather ridge past the Doubtful Lake overlook to Sahale Glacier Camp (about 5.9 mi and 3,940 ft of gain from the trailhead, ~7,600 ft). From camp, traverse east across the boulder/heather plateau below Sahale Glacier (passing roughly a dozen established camp pads), downclimb a steep snowfield (whippet or axe useful, can be firm/icy into midsummer), then traverse east to gain Sahale Peak's sharp southeast ridge. Follow a cairned climber's trail down the ridge, negotiating one short 4th-class step, into a scree/talus gully that drops to a snowfield around 6,600 ft. Cross this snowfield into Horseshoe Basin, traverse a wide ledge at ~6,600 ft rising gradually to ~6,800 ft at the ruins of the old Black Warrior mine, then continue on loose scree/talus contouring to a stance south/southeast of Horseshoe Peak below the crest of Ripsaw Ridge. Lower Horseshoe Basin option (more direct, more elevation loss/regain): from Cascade Pass, drop east into Pelton Basin (established camp; reliable water at Doubtful Creek/Pelton Basin — fill up here, since Horseshoe Basin's own water is contaminated by historic mine tailings and should not be drunk) and work cross-country toward the Black Warrior mine gully, a narrow (~8-ft-wide) rock dike dropping about 100 ft to the Horseshoe Basin side: Class 3 at the top, a short Class 4 downward step to an alcove with old mining equipment stashed in it, then continuing Class 3 but loose and exposed. From the basin floor (~6,600 ft) contour northeast then east on slabs below the Davenport Glacier to reach the base of Ripsaw Ridge below the summit notch. Camping is prohibited in Horseshoe Basin itself, so most parties base at Sahale Glacier Camp or Pelton Basin and day-trip the peak from there — for a round trip of about 14 miles (22.5 km). Either way, expect extended travel on loose talus/scree and slabs with real fall exposure, a snow crossing that wants an axe (crampons in early season), and route-finding by cairn/climber's trail rather than maintained tread once past Sahale Arm or Pelton Basin.
approach_variant_names: Sahale Arm, the secret gully, and the mining-equipment alcove
current.descent: Reverse the approach. From the base of the gully/ledge leading to Horseshoe's summit, scramble about 10 ft of Class 3/4 to a ledge that angles diagonally up the south face to an obvious cleft just below the true summit, exiting on a loose Class 3/4 ledge to the highpoint — a small, roughly one-meter-square notch atop Ripsaw Ridge. There is a solid rock horn on the east side of the notch that serves as the natural rappel anchor (parties also build a small gear anchor from a few cams if a horn sling is absent or worn). One rappel of roughly 100 ft (about 30 m) down the south-face ledge system returns you to the notch/gully below the summit: a 30 m rope reaches close to the bottom, with maybe the last 10 ft needing an easy downclimb, while a 60 m rope (doubled) or a single-strand 60 m lower reaches with rope to spare for a clean single rappel. There is no fixed/bolted hardware here — it's a natural horn and/or gear anchor, so carry a few cams as backup. From the base of the rappel, reverse whichever approach line was used: descend the loose gully/ledge back into Horseshoe Basin, re-cross the ~6,600-ft snowfield, and either regain Sahale Peak's ridge and the Sahale Arm Trail back to Cascade Pass, or climb back out of Pelton Basin over Cascade Pass to the trailhead. Loose, exposed rock on the summit ledges is the main descent hazard (helmet recommended, and manage rope carefully to avoid dislodging blocks); the long snow/scree/slab travel back to camp or the trailhead is otherwise straightforward but sustained.
current.detailed_rack: A light alpine rock rack is sufficient for the single technical pitch — a small-to-mid set of cams and a few stoppers/slings for gear placements and to back up the summit rap anchor; some solo/small parties have rope-soloed or simul-climbed the short pitch with a 60m rope.
rack: Small rock rack: stoppers + finger-to-hand cams (~0.3–0.75in) for the crux
30m rope (minimum) for the short roped section
2-3 slings for a hand line/anchor (sling a horn or chockstone; no fixed anchors)
current.pro_needs: A few small cams (~0.3-0.75) and a set of stoppers protect the short 5.2 crux near the summit notch; good small cam placements and solid stopper constrictions have both been reported. No fixed anchors — use a slung horn or chockstone for the rappel/lower.
current.rope_note: Class 3 dike with a Class 4 down-step; published descriptions note it requires a little bit of roped climbing (half a pitch) — a short rope suffices.

name: Hottentot
beta: P1 climbs past bolts to chains at roughly 5.10+. P2 moves right and up a slab reported as possibly 5.12 and not freed as of 2015, so the pitch's grade and completion status are unresolved.
overview: The crag's hardest-rated line, starting from the rightmost position: a bolted 5.10+ first pitch to chains, then a right-trending second pitch onto a slab whose grade and free-climbing status were unconfirmed as of the last documented ascent (2015).

current.approach: Summertime Crag uses a different trailhead than the other four areas' shared Blue Lake approach. From Winthrop, drive west on SR-20 through Mazama toward Washington Pass (or, coming from Seattle, continue past Washington Pass toward Mazama on SR-20); park at a small pullout on the east side of the highway, just before the larger 'Spires Gully' parking area used to access the Early Winters Spires from the east. From the pullout, descend off the road down through trees, cross Early Winters Creek, follow it briefly downstream, then climb up-slope and contour left to reach the crag — about a 20-25 minute walk with minimal elevation change. The crag stays shaded until mid-afternoon in summer, making it a popular warm-weather alternative when Mazama-area cragging runs hot.
current.descent: Lower/rappel from the P1 chains is documented; the descent from the P2 slab is unknown — verify current beta before attempting the full route.
current.detailed_rack: Bolted P1 to chains — standard quickdraws suffice. P2 is also bolted, with a longer gap past its crux where a piton has pulled out.
current.pro_needs: Both pitches are bolted. On P2 a piton past the crux has come out and was not replaced, so the gap before the last couple of bolts is longer; P2's grade is still unconfirmed.

name: Hourglass Gully (Winter)
beta: Begin at Lake Serene trailhead, ascend 2,000 feet through forest to the lake (4.1 miles), then climb steeply southeast toward the summit. The Hourglass Gully presents 40-60 degree snow and ice, with a crux 60-degree pitch on the East Ridge. The gully constricts dramatically near the exit with near-vertical sections. Timing is critical; the window for this route is narrow (early March through early May). After May, melted conditions expose loose rock and create severe bushwhacking challenges.
overview: A classic winter alpine ascent of Mount Index's Main Peak via a steep gully and exposed ridge, offering 1,900 feet of technical snow/ice climbing with significant avalanche and rockfall hazard.

current.approach: Start at the Lake Serene Trailhead and follow Trail #1068 about 4 miles and 2,000 ft of gain to Lake Serene, then traverse talus and boulders around the west side of the lake to its south end. From there head east to a saddle and climb the ridge/gully system southwest of it toward Main Peak, the massif's highest and most technical summit (~5,991 ft). Expect over 6,000 ft of total elevation gain, dense brush and small cliffs on the ridge above the lake, and steep snow in the gully higher up; most parties plan for a 15+ hour car-to-car day or an overnight.
approach_variant_names: Lake Serene Trail #1068, south-end saddle, southwest ridge
current.descent: The descent mirrors the ascent route but is significantly more technical. On the upper East Ridge, climbers set up two 30-meter rappels using existing rap slings in trees. Descending the Hourglass Gully in spring conditions often involves boot-skiing down 40-50 degree slopes with small wet slides. The steep constriction requires careful down-climbing or short rappels. The ridge traverse back to the lake saddle is exposed with 1,000-foot drops to the northeast side. Return to Lake Serene via the approach slope and descend the 4.1-mile trail by headlamp if a very early start was not made.
current.detailed_rack: Two 30-meter ropes (single-rope rappels, doubled for security), dynamic belay anchors or pickets at rap stations. Rock protection: slings for trees (abundant), quickdraws for anchors. Ice screws (optional, for belayed pitches if team prefers; not typical for this route).
rack: 2×30m ropes for rappels
Snow pickets/deadman anchors
Slings for tree anchors
current.pro_needs: Protection is tree-based and natural feature slings; climbers typically clip existing rap slings on descent or place slings around large trees. Rock is granodiorite; belay anchors should be bombproof trees or solid rock features. No bolts; this is entirely natural protection and tree anchors.
bivy: Lake Serene basin and the talus under the Norwegian Buttresses
current.rope_note: Confirmed as Mount Index's Main Peak, Hourglass Gully (Winter), Grade III/1,900 ft. Class 4/low 5th rock plus a short section of 60+ degree snow/ice/tree climbing on the East Ridge, which is often rappelled on descent. Snow pickets and tree slings are the primary protection, not a rock rack. Ice tools/crampons required.

name: House Buttress
beta: The route begins in a shallow, down-sloping depression with awkward climbing off two fixed pins, then follows the crest as directly as possible over several rock steps and across two significant notches to the summit, with the crux (5.9) typically encountered higher on the route. The climbing is of lower quality than on the Blue Buttress, and protection is hard to find in places. It is also notably longer than its neighbor — subsequent parties have reported as many as 12-17 roped pitches, and its character resembles the South Arete of South Early Winters Spire, stretched to over a thousand feet.
overview: A longer, looser-rock alpine ridge line up the other of Poster Peak's two northeast buttresses, first free-soloed by Steve House in about 45 minutes in the summer of 2003.

current.approach: Shared with Blue's Buttress: park at the 'Hairpin' pullout on Highway 20 near Washington Pass, follow the trail toward Kangaroo Pass for about half a mile, then split off up the drainage toward Poster Peak's buttresses. House Buttress is the first (northernmost) buttress reached, before the traverse over to Blue's Buttress. Approach time is roughly 1 hour.
current.descent: From the summit, follow the short southwest ridge onto easy, scrambling terrain, then work southeast to an obvious short couloir. Descend the couloir and contour back around toward the base of the buttresses to rejoin the approach trail. As with Blue's Buttress, expect loose rock and talus on this walk-off.
current.pro_needs: Protection is reported as harder to find than on Blue's Buttress; parties should expect to run it out in places and plan gear placements conservatively.

name: Northeast Buttress (North Peak)
beta: This is the line Tatum and Loudon took in 1904 and it remains the trade route on the North Peak. From a ridge camp near the border monument at roughly 6,300-6,400 ft, drop to the 5,800 ft saddle at the head of the north cirque, then climb the lower snowfield at an easy angle before the middle snowfield steepens enough to want crampons and an axe. Above the snow the route breaks onto loose Class 3 rock ramps and gullies, threading up and right to gain the northeast ridge crest. The ridge is generally Class 2-3, but around 7,600 ft a section of the connecting ledge has eroded away, leaving a short, badly exposed Class 4 traverse on loose, wet, dirty, down-sloping holds — the psychological crux of the climb. Above that it is attention-grabbing 4th class on sharp, unfractured Hozomeen chert to the summit block. The whole route is graded 'easy' and climbs nothing hard, but nothing on it is casual: the consensus across trip reports is that a fall is not survivable and the rock will not hold protection.
overview: The historic original route to Hozomeen's North Peak summit and one of the peak's easier scrambling lines, first climbed in 1904.

current.approach: There is no US road to Hozomeen. From the Trans-Canada Highway (BC Hwy 1) take Exit 168 at Hope, British Columbia, follow Flood-Hope Road onto Silver-Skagit Road, and drive roughly 34 miles / 55 km of gravel south through Skagit Valley Provincial Park to the Skyline II trailhead — about an hour and a quarter. Verify road and border status first: Silver-Skagit Road has been closed at km 6 for wildfire since 24 July 2026, and NPS has prohibited both vehicle and foot traffic across the boundary at Hozomeen since 2020, with no end date given on the park's fire-closure page updated 14 September 2026. From Skyline II, climb the trail roughly 8 miles and 4,000 ft to the Hozomeen Ridge junction, then turn south on the Hozomeen Ridge Trail over rolling terrain to a camp near the Monument 74 high point at about 6,345 ft, 10.5 miles in. Take water from the three creeks in the forest below Hozomeen Ridge — there is no running water again until you are south of the border. From camp the climb begins by dropping about 545 ft to the 5,800 ft saddle at the head of the north cirque. A shorter but much nastier alternative starts at the Hozomeen ranger station, follows the short Trail of the Obelisk loop, then bushwhacks east up the overgrown border swath past a swamp and gains about 3,000 ft to a col near 6,300 ft before joining the ridge; it saves miles and costs hours.
approach_variant_names: The long way: the ridge trail from the north to a camp near the boundary high point
The short way: the border swath from the ranger station
current.descent: Descend exactly the way you came up. Downclimb the summit blocks and the exposed 7,600 ft step facing inward, taking the same line you climbed — do not try to shortcut the ledge system, because the north cirque side is undercut and the alternatives cliff out. Below the rock, downclimb the upper snowfield facing in, then plunge-step and glissade the lower snowfield to the saddle. Cold, firm morning snow that took crampons cleanly will be soft and rotten on the way down; the same slope that felt secure at 07:00 can be a wet-slide problem at 15:00, and late-season moats at the snow-rock margin are a real trap. Regain the ridge to camp, then reverse the Hozomeen Ridge and Skyline II trails. Parties who camped and descended in one push report roughly six hours from summit back to the trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: Not a rock rack route. Parties that bring a rope carry a 30 m half or twin line, four or five slings, a couple of medium nuts and two locking carabiners — enough to sling a horn for a short lower over the 7,600 ft step. Do not expect that gear to be usable more broadly: reports from this face and the neighbouring routes are consistent that the Hozomeen chert takes protection poorly and that placements are mostly ornamental.
current.pro_needs: Effectively none, and that is the point. The climbing is easy enough to solo and loose enough that most parties judge a rope a liability rather than an asset above the snow. Protect yourself with snow technique and movement discipline, not hardware.

name: Southwest Buttress (North Peak)
beta: A climber reached roughly 60% of the route on a third try before retreating, free-climbing a crux pitch that earlier parties had aided. The second ascent, in 1998, involved a summit-day round trip of about 12 hours from bivouac back to the car. Treat all of this as thin, second-hand history rather than current beta.
overview: A serious, poorly-protected Grade IV technical rock route on the North Peak's southwest side; very few successful ascents are reported, and protection is difficult.

name: West Face (North Peak)
beta: A genuine Cascade backcountry big-wall problem rather than a route in the usual sense. The line takes the left-facing corner systems that lead directly to the summit, with rope-stretcher pitches through the 6-10 range and a leftward traverse of the wall's distinctive tiger-stripe ledges to avoid the overhanging upper section, reaching the summit ridge about 100 ft from the top. Twelve pitches, climbed all free at 5.9, with one shallow piton placed and removed and no bolts on the entire route - Cascade ground-up ethics applied to a wall that barely accepts hardware. The first ascensionists' own summary is the best warning available: the face is very large, much steeper than it appears from below, the rock is friable, and there are almost no protection cracks, even for thin pitons. One published account rates the line V 5.9+ R/X rather than the published IV 5.9, and the R/X reflects reality better than the number does. What the rock lacks in solidity and protection it partly returns in a plethora of in-cut features, which climb well where they are attached. Larson and Wehrly bivouacked atop pitch 10, about 100 m below the summit.
overview: A Grade IV, 5.9 technical rock route on the North Peak's west face, very difficult to protect and among the hardest routes on the mountain.

current.approach: A two-stage approach and the second stage is the part that stops people. Day one is a long haul of 11-plus miles under heavy loads from the road to a camp just north of the peak - the same Hozomeen Ridge / border-swath ground used by the north-side scrambling routes, reached from Silver-Skagit Road out of Hope, B.C. From that camp the approach to the base took the first ascent party a tedious and painstaking 4.5 hours: downclimb a loose third-class gully, which the party described as dangerous but the lesser of the two evils, then cross several precipitous rocky ribs and steep, unstable ground to traverse into the launch point below the wall. Budget the base approach as a half-day objective in its own right and do it in daylight. Confirm the NPS border-gate status before planning; the crossing at Hozomeen has been closed to vehicles and foot traffic since 2020, with no end date given on the park's fire-closure page updated 14 September 2026.
approach_variant_names: Ridge camp north of the peak, then the traverse down and across to the foot of the wall
current.descent: From the summit, take the easy north-side ground: reverse the Northeast Buttress / North Route line, downclimbing the Class 2-3 northeast ridge, treating the short very exposed Class 4 eroded segment near 7,600 ft with maximum care, then descending the north cirque snowfields to the saddle and back to camp. In late summer, when this route is in condition, those snowfields will be thin or gone, leaving loose rock in their place - carry an axe anyway if any snow remains, and expect the descent to be slower than the grade suggests. Rappelling the west face is not a plan: with almost no protection cracks, every anchor would be a construction project on rotten rock.
current.detailed_rack: Reports do not publish a rack list, and the honest reason is that the wall barely accepts protection. What is documented: the first ascent placed and removed exactly one shallow piton across all 12 pitches and placed no bolts. Plan a broad, light, alpine trad rack - a full set of small-to-medium cams, doubles in the sizes you trust, a full set of nuts including brass, several thin pitons and a hammer, and a generous number of long slings for threading and slinging the in-cut features that constitute most of the usable protection. Bring double ropes for the rope-stretcher pitches and for any emergency retreat. Nothing on this list should be relied on; the first ascent description of the protection on the neighbouring Hozomeen wall - infrequent and mostly ornamental - applies here too.
current.pro_needs: Sparse, poor and often absent. The defining feature of the Zorro Face is that there are almost no protection cracks, even for thin pitons, across a very large and steeper-than-expected wall of friable metamorphosed basalt. This is R/X terrain in one published account's rating. Leaders must be comfortable running out easy-to-moderate 5th class ground on rock that may detach, and the belays are as much of a problem as the pitches. Do not treat 5.9 as the difficulty - the difficulty is 5.9 with nothing between you and the belay.

name: East Ridge
beta: The historic first-ascent route. Scramble the ridge crest (Class 3/4, generally linking clumps of trees) over an intimidating Class 4 step to a false summit, downclimb into a notch (watch a loose block here), traverse a crumbly Class 2 ledge above a big cliff, then climb a blocky headwall to the summit block's east face. The crux is a short, well-protected, roughly 3-move low-5th (~5.3) curving dihedral just below the summit.
overview: The original 1915 line to Huckleberry's summit: a long Class 3/4 ridge-crest scramble to a jagged notch, then a short, well-protected low-5th-class dihedral through the summit block's east face.

current.approach: From the PCT North Trailhead at Snoqualmie Pass (~3,000 ft), hike the PCT northbound via Kendall Pass and the Kendall Katwalk to Ridge Lake, then continue past Alaska Pass and around Joe Lake to the rolling meadows of Huckleberry Flats, roughly 10-11 miles one-way. Most parties camp at Ridge Lake, about 7 miles and 2,700 ft of gain from the trailhead. From Huckleberry Flats, leave the PCT and climb to the base of the east ridge at roughly 6,100 ft, where a rocky buttress marks the start of the technical ridge. From the Joe Lake stretch of the PCT, the east slope's heather and blueberry bench leads to the 6,000 ft shoulder and the crest; there is no need to cut onto the loose south-face gully (August).
approach_variant_names: PCT past the Kendall Katwalk to a point due east of the summit, then straight up
current.descent: From the summit, downclimb back to the notch and rappel off a large pile of rocks with tat on it. A second, lower rappel on the ridge gets you past the 4th-class step and back to easier scrambling terrain leading to the base of the route.
current.detailed_rack: An alpine half rack — stoppers (roughly #2-#10) and small cams (about 0.5-0.75 in) — plus a handful of runners (a mix of singles and doubles). A 60 m rope is needed; a 40 m rope is too short for a full rappel.
current.pro_needs: Light rack for a short, well-protected low-5th crux; loose rock throughout the ridge and summit block demands care with placements and stance.

name: West Face
beta: There is no true walk-up to Huckleberry's summit. The mountain's original (and for decades only) route climbs class 3-4 terrain along the ridge crest with a short, exposed low-5th-class step to top out the summit block; two later technical lines — a 5.7 South Face and a 5.6 West Face first climbed in 2001 — are more sustained rock routes. Nearly all parties, including strong scramblers, bring a rope and light rack to protect and rappel the final block.
overview: Huckleberry Mountain (6,320-6,340 ft) is a small but striking andesite peak on the Cascade Crest ridgeline between Mount Thomson and Chikamin Peak, about 5 miles northeast of Snoqualmie Pass in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness. It is not near the Middle Fork Snoqualmie/Dutch Miller Gap trail system — it's reached from the Pacific Crest Trail, which traverses its south and east slopes past Kendall Katwalk, Ridge Lake, and Alaska Mountain. The summit sits on the King/Kittitas county line. Two historic lines reach the same technical summit block: an older west-side gully (now less favored due to rockfall) and the more popular East Ridge.

current.approach: Park at the PCT North Trailhead at Snoqualmie Pass (I-90 Exit 52, large lot off SR 906/Alpental Rd; Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass required). Head north on the Pacific Crest Trail; most parties cut the corner via the Commonwealth Basin/Red Pass climbers' shortcut, which rejoins the PCT and trims about a mile off the standard trail. Climb the well-graded PCT switchbacks up to Kendall Katwalk (roughly 5 miles and 2,600 ft of gain from the trailhead) — a dramatic ledge blasted into a cliff face with real exposure in a fall-on-snow scenario early season. Continue north on the PCT past Ridge Lake and Gravel Lake, skirting the base of Alaska Mountain, to where the trail runs above Joe Lake, about 10 miles from the pass. For the West Route, leave the trail at a flowery meadow northeast of Joe Lake and head up a talus slope into the basin below the west face, which is clearly visible from there. Alternatively, take the Gold Creek Trail to Joe Lake and hike upslope to the PCT. Water is reliable at Ridge Lake and Gravel Lake, and at Joe Lake below the trail. Hazards on the approach include lingering snow on north-facing benches into July, loose rock in the approach gullies and talus once off-trail, and route-finding in poor visibility. Because of the length, many parties split this into 2-3 days with a camp at Ridge Lake or Gravel Lake.
current.descent: Rappel the summit block (60m rope recommended) down to the notch, then reverse the gully/ridge down to Huckleberry Flats and rejoin the PCT back to the trailhead; there is no simple walk-off.
current.detailed_rack: A light alpine rack is typical: a handful of small-to-medium stoppers, one or two small cams, and several slings for horn/block anchors, plus a 60-meter rope to protect and rappel the summit block.
rack: Small-to-medium stoppers
One or two small cams
Several slings for horn/block rappel anchor
60m rope to protect and rappel the summit block
current.pro_needs: Protection needs are modest — small stoppers and cams protect the short technical step to the top of the summit block, and slings back up horns or blocks for the rappel anchor.
bivy: Ridge Lake and Gravel Lake, PCT beyond Kendall Katwalk
Alaska Lake and Joe Lake, Gold Creek
current.rope_note: The West Face goes at 5.6; bring a 60m rope to rappel the summit block.

name: South Ridge
beta: A popular side trip from the Cascade Pass area or via the Ptarmigan Traverse. The south ridge route involves crossing a steep snow band and broken granite above Kool-Aid Lake, then class 2-3 scrambling with moderate exposure along the summit ridge. Route finding can be tricky; descend via the same route.
overview: Hurry-up Peak (7,821 ft) lies on the Skagit-Chelan county line at the northern end of the Ptarmigan Traverse, just south of Cascade Pass and Cache Col, between Magic Mountain and Spider Mountain (its line parent). It is not part of the Sahale-Boston/Horseshoe Basin group on the opposite side of the pass; instead it's reached from a Kool-Aid Lake camp on the traverse's first day. A quiet, seldom-solo-targeted scramble, it is usually tagged as a short side trip by parties already committed to the Ptarmigan Traverse rather than climbed on its own.

current.approach: Start at the Cascade Pass Trailhead (~3,600 ft) at the end of Cascade River Road (about 23 miles of pavement then gravel from Marblemount; the upper gravel section is gated and typically doesn't open until snow clears, often not until late June/July). From the trailhead, follow the well-graded, heavily-used Cascade Pass Trail 3.7 miles and about 1,800 ft of gain, switchbacking up through forest and avalanche-path meadows to Cascade Pass (5,392 ft) — the last reliable trailside water is at the creek crossings low on the trail, so top off bottles before the switchbacks. At the pass, leave the maintained tread and pick up the climbers' path/boot track heading south-southeast, making a rising traverse across snow or heather on the flanks of Mixup Peak to the base of the Cache Glacier (~6,000 ft); this stretch is loose, choosy, and crosses several snow patches that can be firm in early morning. Ascend moderate glacier/snow slopes (crevasses can open by late summer — rope up if the party isn't comfortable soloing them) to the notch at Cache Col (6,900 ft). From the col, descend and traverse south-southeast about 1 mile over loose rock and heather benches, crossing occasional snowfields, down to Kool-Aid Lake (6,120 ft), the standard base camp for this side of the Ptarmigan Traverse and the only dependable water source in the basin (may be partly frozen early season). Car-to-camp is roughly 5-6 miles with about 3,300 ft of gain, generally a half-day carrying overnight gear. From camp, the peak itself is climbed as a side trip: head up toward Hurry-up Peak's south/southwest flank, crossing a band of steep snow around 7,100 ft (carry an axe/crampons even mid-summer) before gaining broken granite slabs and the south ridge crest; follow the crest/upper gully system with sustained Class 2-3 scrambling and a couple of exposed but short moves along the summit ridge to the 7,821 ft top — about 1 mile and 1,400-1,500 ft above camp, roughly 1-1.5 hours for a fit party.
approach_variant_names: Cache Col to Kool-Aid Lake
current.descent: This is a walk-off/downclimb — no rappelling. From the summit, reverse the ascent line back down the south ridge/gully system, downclimbing the same Class 2-3 granite terrain and re-crossing the steep snow band near 7,100 ft (plunge-step or glissade if conditions allow, but keep the axe out given the exposure just above), back down to Kool-Aid Lake camp — about 3-3.5 hours round trip from camp is typical for the whole side-trip. From camp, descend by reversing the approach: climb back up to Cache Col, down the Cache Glacier snow slopes, traverse back around Mixup Peak's flanks to Cascade Pass, then descend the maintained Cascade Pass Trail to the trailhead. No technical descent hazards beyond the approach terrain itself — main concerns are the steep snow crossing near 7,100 ft (harder and icier in early season or late day when it's refrozen) and losing the boot path on the granite benches between Kool-Aid Lake and the ridge, which has multiple similar-looking gully options.
current.detailed_rack: No rock gear required for the scramble.
current.pro_needs: None on the standard route.

name: Iceman
beta: Climbs a steep face on good holds to a bolt guarding a thin finger-crack move, then finishes on horizontal cracks into an awkward but enjoyable left-facing corner. Mixed protection (3 bolts plus small-to-mid cams) makes it the trad line of the three Ice Box routes.
overview: A one-pitch 5.10a/b line up the shaded Ice Box (Left Side) buttress, the 'dead middle' finger-crack/roof line splitting sport routes Route C and Route D.

current.approach: Park at the apex of the hairpin turn on SR-20 below Washington Pass. Follow the climbers' trail up toward Quicksilver Slab and Spire Gully, then cut right into a dry creek bed and climb the slabs above it into the Ice Box. The upper, entrance slab has a fixed line; the lower slab does not. Both are smooth and slippery, and worse when wet.
current.descent: From the top anchor, lower on a single strand or rappel with a 60m rope directly back to the base of the route; no walk-off is required for this single-pitch line.
current.detailed_rack: 3 fixed bolts protect the crux face and finger-crack section; supplement with a small rack of cams from about BD #0.3 to #1 for the horizontal-crack and corner finish. A single 60m rope and standard quickdraws/alpine draws are sufficient for this one-pitch route.
current.pro_needs: Mixed protection — 3 bolts plus a handful of small-to-medium cams (0.3-1 BD equivalent) placed in the horizontal cracks and finishing corner.

name: Ruth-Icy Traverse (Northwest Ridge, via Ruth Mountain)
beta: From Hannegan Pass, parties gain Ruth Mountain (via its glacier/snow slopes), then descend south and west from Ruth's summit toward a gully on its west side and continue down to the Ruth-Icy Saddle, from which Icy Peak is clearly visible. From the saddle, cross talus and slabs below a rock ridge onto Icy's glacier and climb firm snow to a notch just west of Icy's Northwest Spire, near 6,500 ft; from there, 2nd-3rd class climbing on mostly good rock leads to a 100-ft 4th-class summit gully and the Northwest summit, which holds the register. The true (Southeast) summit takes a harder, less often climbed line from the notch between the Northwest and Southeast summits up the Southeast Peak's steep, loose, very exposed Northwest Ridge to a Class 4 knife-edge summit ridge.
overview: A committing high-ridge traverse linking Ruth Mountain to Icy Peak's true (Southeast) summit via the Ruth-Icy Saddle and Icy Peak's Northwest Ridge — a full alpine day combining glacier travel, loose ridge scrambling, and an exposed Class 4 summit ridge.

current.approach: Drive Mt. Baker Highway (SR 542) to Hannegan Pass Road (FR 32) and follow it to its end at the Hannegan Trailhead/Campground (~3,100 ft, at the end of Ruth Creek Road). Hike the Hannegan Pass Trail roughly 4 miles and about 2,000 ft up to Hannegan Pass (~5,050 ft), then continue on climbers' route/snow up Ruth Mountain's flank toward its summit before beginning the traverse.
current.descent: Downclimb or rappel (a 75-ft/23m rope has been used for short belays and lowers) the steeper ridge sections back to the Ruth-Icy Saddle. From the saddle, re-ascend or contour around Ruth Mountain's south ridge, then descend snow/glacier slopes back to Hannegan Pass and follow the maintained trail down to the Hannegan Trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: Rope (a 75-ft/23m rope has been used for short belays/lowers on the ridge), a few snow pickets for the glacier sections, and a light rock rack for the 4th-class ridge and summit gully.
current.pro_needs: Snow pickets protect the Ruth and Icy Glacier crossings; the 4th-class summit ridge/gully takes slings and small gear over generally sound rock.
bivy: Ruth Arm ridge camps below the Ruth Glacier
Hannegan trailhead, end of the Ruth Creek road
Notch bivy on the Ruth-Icy ridge

name: Southwest Route / Icy Glacier
beta: Most common Icy Peak route: from Hannegan Pass trailhead, ascend to Ruth Mountain, traverse glacier and snow south and west to approximate 6500 ft, then ascend talus and snow through southwest gully to summit. Route involves navigating a horizontal crevasse near the top of the glacier, aiming for notch on southwest ridgeline at 6600 ft, then south through glacier's west face. Final summit push is a 100-foot Class 4 gully with mostly good rock.
overview: Icy Peak is a remote, heavily glaciated summit at the head of the Nooksack Cirque in the North Cascades, geologically a remnant of the ancient Hannegan Caldera volcano. Small glaciers cling to every flank, with an icefall dropping into the northeast cirque. The peak has two summits — a lower, more-frequently-visited Northwest Peak and the true, higher Southeast summit (7,073 ft), reached by extra scrambling beyond the top of this route's gully — separated by an exposed ridge. High connecting ridges tie it to Ruth Mountain, Seahpo Peak, and Mount Shuksan. It sees very light traffic (summit registers suggest roughly one party a year), and most parties combine it with an ascent of Ruth Mountain on the same trip since the two share the same approach via Hannegan Pass.

current.approach: Start at the Hannegan Pass Trailhead (Trail #674) at road's end on FS Road 32 (Hannegan Pass Road), off SR 542 (Mt. Baker Highway), elevation ~3,100 ft. Hike Trail #674 roughly 4 miles, switchbacking up through forest along Ruth Creek to Hannegan Pass (5,066 ft), gaining ~2,000 ft. The signed Hannegan Camp (~3.5 mi in) is the last reliable water on the trail — fill up there, as there is no running water past it for the rest of the route. From the pass, leave the maintained trail and go cross-country south, climbing open heather meadows and scattered timber onto Ruth Mountain's north side (3rd-class terrain through trees in spots), then rope up and ascend the moderate slopes of the Ruth Glacier — crevasses open up here in late season, especially on the upper mountain — to Ruth Mountain's summit (7,115 ft). Most parties treat this as a 5–6 hour trailhead-to-camp day, camping on Ruth's summit plateau or in the saddle beyond it. From camp, descend Ruth's south/west side about 1,400 ft from the summit (about 900 ft from the notch camp); there are two common lines down — a steep, loose gully some parties call the 'death gully,' or safer heather slopes and a game trail on climber's left (2nd–3rd class) — down to the Ruth–Icy saddle (~5,700 ft). From the saddle, traverse talus and slabs below a rock ridge to gain the Icy Glacier, rope up again, and climb the glacier's northwest slope gradually southeast, keeping the rock ridge on your left and crevasses on your right, to about 6,500 ft. Traverse the upper glacier below Icy's west face, skirting the west notch (watch for a bergschrund near the top some seasons), to reach a notch/saddle west of Icy's Northwest Spire (~6,500 ft). From there climb roughly 500 ft of 2nd–3rd class talus and snow up Icy's south side to the base of a light-colored, ~100-ft 4th-class summit gully with solid jugs and ledges; this leads to the northwest summit. Note the true high point is a separate southeast tower about 11 ft higher, reached by additional 3rd/4th class scrambling — many parties only tag the northwest summit, which holds the register. Hazards throughout: crevasses on both the Ruth and Icy Glaciers, occasional rockfall on Icy's south-side scramble terrain, black flies and mosquitoes on the lower trail in summer, and essentially no water source after Hannegan Camp. A few moves in the summit gully feel low-fifth class rather than straightforward 4th class, depending on the exact line chosen.
approach_variant_names: Hannegan Pass, over Ruth Mountain, then the Icy Glacier's northwest slope to the west notch
current.descent: Descent reverses the ascent line. Off the summit gully, parties either downclimb the 4th-class rock (described as casual with solid holds) or rig a single rappel: a 60m rope doubled gives about 30m (100 ft) of rope per side, matching the gully's height, anchored on slings/webbing around a rock horn at the top — this is a natural anchor only (no bolts/fixed chains reported), so inspect and back up existing tat before trusting it. From the base of the gully, downclimb the 2nd–3rd class talus/snow back to the Icy Glacier saddle, re-rope and re-cross the Icy Glacier reversing the ascent line, then traverse back to the Ruth–Icy saddle. From there it's roughly 1,400 ft of regain back up to Ruth Mountain's summit (about 900 ft to the notch camp) — the sting in the tail of this traverse — before descending Ruth's north side and the Ruth Glacier back to Hannegan Pass, and hiking the 4-mile trail out to the trailhead. This is a long day (done in a single push it is typically 15-20 hours car-to-car, with a fast party moving for about 12 of them) with significant elevation loss-then-regain between Icy and Ruth; carry a stove or plan water carefully since there's no reliable source between Hannegan Camp and the trailhead on the way out. Watch for loose rock in the summit gully and standard crevasse/glacier hazards in reverse on both glaciers.
current.detailed_rack: A few small-to-mid cams and nuts plus 3-4 slings for the short Class 4 summit gully and to inspect/back up the fixed horn-sling rappel anchor, on top of standard glacier travel gear (rope per rope team, pickets, crevasse-rescue kit) for the Ruth and Icy glacier crossings.
current.pro_needs: Minimal rock pro; glacier protection as conditions dictate.
bivy: Ruth Arm ridge camps below the Ruth Glacier
Hannegan trailhead, end of the Ruth Creek road
Notch bivy on the Ruth-Icy ridge

name: Imbibing the Movements on Human Destiny
beta: Pitch 1 (5.10-): starts with a thin corner crack (~5.8) protected by small cams; after ~35 ft, bolted climbing leads to a ledge, then a short, well-protected 5.10 section reaches the first anchors. Pitch 2 (5.9-): enjoyable slabby climbing above leads to the top of the wall.
overview: A two-pitch corner-crack-to-slab route at the very bottom of the East Face trail.

current.approach: At the very bottom of the trail to the lower East Face climbs, near the left corner of the orange/green face — a corner crack just right of the trees marking the start of Black Systems Solar.
current.descent: Chain anchors atop both pitches; rappel or lower each pitch, or in two stages from the top.
current.detailed_rack: 13 bolts total plus gear placements to 2 inches (small cams) for the opening corner crack; chain anchors atop both pitches.
current.pro_needs: Small cams to 2 inches for the thin opening corner crack; the remainder is bolt-protected.

name: Incoming
beta: Face climbing builds to a constriction (crux) and small roof with great holds; hard sections can be bypassed. Sits in the shade all day with excellent views from the anchors. Located west side, left of a large overhanging feature.
overview: Sport climb on Megadike North.

current.approach: The Dikes sit in the Umatilla National Forest's Walla Walla Ranger District, in the East Fork Touchet River valley near Ski Bluewood, southeast Washington — not near the Snake River. Access is via North Touchet Road out of Dayton, WA, paved for roughly the first 15-16 miles before becoming gravel Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary; the road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter, but snow on the crags and approach slopes keeps the climbing season to roughly May-October, sometimes from April. Approaches are very short and roadside: the south Megadike is reached by parking near a bridge 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and scrambling directly up the steep hillside above the bridge abutment, while Weeping Wall and Joe's Rock are similar short pullout-to-cliff scrambles at 1.1 and 2.0 miles past the same trailhead respectively. The area is lightly visited and faint-trailed, and the basalt is notably loose/fractured, requiring routine loose-rock cleaning. This route is on Megadike North: pull over at 1.1 miles beyond the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead, at the spot on the left (SE side) where a dirt road joins the pavement, or drive on to 1.2 miles and use the large pull-off. Cross the main road and pick up the approach trail between the two parking spots, marked by a short steep drainage topped with a downed tree.
current.descent: Lower from the 3-bolt chain anchor on a single strand (well within a 60m rope for this 80 ft route).
current.detailed_rack: 14 bolts to a 3-bolt chain anchor — bring a full rack of draws for this longer pitch.
current.pro_needs: Fully bolted (14 bolts).
current.rope_note: Single-pitch bolted sport route at Megadike North (The Dikes, WA). 70m recommended given Megadike North's walls up to ~120ft.

name: Southwest Slopes (Standard Route)
beta: From a backcountry camp near Indian Pass (5,000 ft) on the Pacific Crest Trail, climbers leave the trail and head up bushy hillside on the peak's southwest/south slopes; the terrain opens up above the brush into Class 2 talus and boulder slopes. The line trends up onto the west ridge and follows it toward the summit block. The ridge holds twin summits close in height -- most parties stop at the west (false) summit where a register sits, but trip reports and elevation checks indicate the east summit is 15-40 feet higher and has better Class 3 scrambling; reaching it requires a short, loose, exposed corkscrew move around onto the peak's southeast face near the top.
overview: The standard non-technical line: a long backpack approach via White Pass to Indian Pass on the PCT, then an off-trail scramble up the peak's south/southwest slopes onto its west ridge, finishing with a short exposed move onto the southeast face to reach the true (east) summit.

current.approach: Drive the Mountain Loop Highway from Darrington (WA-530) about 16 miles, then turn onto Forest Road 49 (Sloan Creek Road) and continue about 6.4 miles to the North Fork Sauk Trailhead (2,070 ft, vault toilet, no potable water). Hike the North Fork Sauk Trail #649 through old-growth forest, passing Red Creek camp (3.5 mi) and Mackinaw Shelter (5 mi), then climbing roughly 3,000 ft over the final miles to the Pacific Crest Trail junction (~8.2 mi from the trailhead). Turn right (southbound) on the PCT and follow it about 0.7 mi to White Pass, then continue about 4 more miles south on the PCT to Indian Pass (~4,962-5,000 ft), the low point/junction with the Indian Creek Trail and the jumping-off point for the peak. Total one-way approach to Indian Pass is roughly 13-14 miles.
current.descent: From the true (east) summit, carefully reverse the short exposed corkscrew move back onto the west ridge/false summit area, then descend the same Class 2 talus and boulder slopes on the south/southwest face used on the ascent, watching for loose rock. Regain the bushy hillside below and return to a camp near Indian Pass. From there, retrace the PCT south to White Pass and drop back onto the North Fork Sauk Trail for the long hike out to the trailhead. No rappels are needed on this route; it is a walk-down of the ascent line.
current.pro_needs: Unroped Class 2 scramble; no fixed protection or rope typically used on the standard line.

name: Indian Mountain Scramble
beta: The easiest (and only documented) line up Indian Mountain is straightforward Class 2 scrambling on open talus and heather slopes above treeline. The crux of the trip is logistical, not technical: a long approach through North Cascades National Park wilderness (Hannegan Pass, the Chilliwack River corridor, and the Whatcom Pass/Brush Creek/Indian Creek drainages), unbridged fords, brushy avalanche-path sections, and finally sustained off-trail cross-country travel to gain the summit ridge. The peak's defining character is its relief, rising more than 4,100 ft above Brush Creek valley in roughly one mile, so the final push feels steep even though no roped climbing is required.
overview: Indian Mountain (7,133 ft) is a remote, rarely climbed summit in the North Cascades National Park backcountry, about 7 miles south of the Canadian border in Whatcom County. It sits in the Chilliwack River drainage — which flows north into Canada, not toward Baker Lake — between Whatcom Pass and Copper Ridge, and gains roughly 4,100 ft above Brush Creek Valley in about a mile, giving it dramatic local relief despite its modest elevation. There is no maintained trail to the summit; it is reached only via a multi-day, largely cross-country approach off the Hannegan Pass/Chilliwack River/Brush Creek trail corridor, and essentially no published trip reports document a specific ascent line.

current.approach: No maintained trail reaches the summit — Indian Mountain is approached cross-country from the Hannegan Pass/Chilliwack River trail system, the only real access into this part of the park. From the Hannegan Trailhead (3,120 ft, end of FR 32/Ruth Creek Road), follow the Hannegan Pass Trail roughly 4-5.6 mi over 5,050-ft Hannegan Pass, then switchback down into the Chilliwack River valley to the Boundary Camp area (about 5.1 mi in) as you cross into North Cascades National Park. Continue down-valley on the Chilliwack River Trail, crossing the river via the hand-pulled 2-person cable car (replaced Oct. 2019), to the Brush Creek Trail junction (roughly 11-12 mi from the trailhead). From there take the Brush Creek Trail, which climbs through the 2022 Brush Creek Fire burn toward Whatcom Pass (about 5.1 mi one-way from the Brush Creek junction). Indian Mountain rises immediately above this corridor; parties leave the trail below or near Whatcom Pass and work up open heather/talus slopes and ridgelines to the summit, with sustained, often brushy or loose route-finding required in both directions. One-way distance to the summit runs roughly 16 miles, making this realistically a 3-5 day objective, most often combined with a broader Whatcom Pass/Copper Ridge trip rather than climbed stand-alone.
current.descent: Reverse the ascent line back down to the Brush Creek/Chilliwack River trail corridor — there is no shorter alternative. Re-cross the Chilliwack River via the cable car and climb back over Hannegan Pass to the trailhead; the round trip runs about 32 miles, so budget contingency time for blowdown in the Brush Creek burn area and possible high water at creek crossings.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rack is required; every source describing this peak's easiest route calls it Class 2 scrambling with no roped climbing.
current.pro_needs: None documented — the route involves no technical protection.
current.rope_note: Remote Class 2-3 scramble in the Skagit Range near Whatcom Peak (North Cascades NP); no route-specific technical beta located. Terrain-based inference: standard scramble unroped, though an ice axe may be useful for snow approach.

name: East Peak (Northeast Ridge to East Face)
beta: The lower northeast ridge section climbs 4th-to-easy-fifth-class (5.4 max) slabs and cracks on excellent rock. It's followed by the crux upper east-face pitch, graded 5.6 X on rock described as horrible, with almost no protection - this is not a route for the average 5.6 climber, and picking the wrong line on the face can be fatal. A 70 m rope and a light alpine rack are needed.
overview: A two-section line up the northeast ridge and east face of Ingalls' East Peak: moderate 4th/low-5th-class ridge climbing gives way to a serious, poorly protected 5.6 X face pitch to the summit.

current.approach: Park at the Esmeralda trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway road and take the Lake Ingalls trail. After about 0.4 mile the Ingalls Way junction bears right, and a second junction near 1.4 miles leads off to Longs Pass; stay on the main trail through Headlight Basin to Ingalls Pass at roughly 3 miles and 6,500 ft, about 2,500 ft of gain.
