Descend into the basin and traverse to Lake Ingalls, taking the higher trail for the shortest way, or the lower fork if you are camping in Headlight Basin. From the lake, head toward the east side of the peak, keeping to the right of the large couloir there. Easy ledges lead to the base of the northeast ridge.
current.descent: Descend by rappelling the East Peak Southwest Face route (3 rap stations) back down to the North-East Peak notch, then reverse the approach terrain to Lake Ingalls and out via Ingalls Pass.
current.detailed_rack: A light alpine rack; published notes say the crux pitch offers almost no protection regardless of what's carried, so extra small gear won't meaningfully change the risk on that pitch.
current.pro_needs: 70 m rope required for the pitch lengths; the crux face pitch protects poorly no matter the rack carried - this is the defining hazard of the route.

name: South Ridge
beta: The South Ridge ascends south-facing aspect of North Peak via mixed terrain and crack systems. Hike broken rock and slabs to broad bench below the large red slab. Two main crack variations: traditional 5.4 on left, 5.6 Beckey variation in middle. Pitches are bolted at anchors (pitches 2-3) with additional slings at pitch 1. Serpentine rock sections are notably slick; helmets recommended above 6,900 ft due to rockfall hazard. Parties of 3-4 fit comfortably on small belay ledges.
overview: The South Ridge of Ingalls Peak is one of the most popular moderate alpine rock climbs in the Teanaway, on excellent reddish peridotite. Several pitches of low-fifth-class climbing on a clean, exposed ridge lead to the main (North) summit, with stunning views of Mount Stuart across the basin.

current.approach: From the Esmeralda Basin/Ingalls Lake Trailhead (end of Teanaway River Road/USFS Rd 9737), take the Ingalls Way Trail (#1390). At about 0.4 mile bear right at the junction onto Ingalls Way (Esmeralda Basin Trail #1394 continues straight); at roughly 1.4 miles pass the Longs Pass junction. The trail climbs steadily through forest and open slopes to Ingalls Pass (~6,500 ft) at about 3.0-3.1 miles, the Alpine Lakes Wilderness boundary and your first full view of Mount Stuart and the Ingalls group. From the pass, drop slightly and traverse climbers'-left across open slabs and talus (a boot path braids through here; stay on durable surfaces where possible) for roughly another mile to Lake Ingalls (6,480 ft), about 4-4.5 miles and ~2,500-2,600 ft of gain from the trailhead. This is the last reliable water before the climb. From the lake's outlet/left (west) side, scramble up class 2-3 slabs and talus, aiming for the obvious cleft/notch splitting North Ingalls Peak from the main (South) summit, working up to about 7,100 ft. A short section of class 4 leads up a gully to a ledge system at the base of the ridge proper - this is where the roped climbing (pitch 1) begins. No creek fords are involved past the lake; the main approach hazards are loose talus/scree on the slabs above the lake and afternoon thunderstorm exposure on the open ridge - start early. Total approach is commonly reckoned at 3-4 hours from the car.
approach_variant_names: Esmeralda Basin trailhead, Ingalls Way over Ingalls Pass to Lake Ingalls
Ingalls Way Alternate #1390.2 through Headlight Basin (the camping branch)
current.descent: Descend by rappelling the South Ridge climbing line itself (or, for parties who diverge, the closely parallel Southwest Face). From the summit it is four rappels on a single 60 m rope, or three with two 60 m ropes, described here for two ropes: (1) a single-strand rappel down the uppermost pitch to a two-bolt anchor on a narrow ledge; (2) a full-length rappel (double-rope length, i.e. using the rope doubled) down to a large ledge/slung boulder near the top of pitch 2 - do not be tempted to skip straight from the summit to the top of pitch 2 in one long rappel, since a crack just below the top anchor is notorious for wedging and stuck ropes have resulted; breaking it at the pitch-3 ledge avoids this; and (3) a final rappel from that ledge down to the base ledges/gully where the climb started. Anchors are a mix of fixed two-bolt stations and natural slung-boulder/horn anchors reinforced with webbing - carry a few extra feet of tat/webbing since the natural anchors get replaced periodically and can be tired. Below the last rappel, downclimb the class 3-4 gully back to the notch and retrace the approach talus/slabs to Lake Ingalls and out via Ingalls Pass.
current.detailed_rack: Small rack to ~2 inches; a single set of cams and a few nuts with slings is typically ample for the 5.4 climbing.
current.pro_needs: Light rack, plenty of slings for the blocky ridge.
bivy: Beverly and De Roux campgrounds and the North Fork Teanaway roadside camps

name: South Peak Scramble
beta: South Peak (7,640 ft) is the southernmost and easiest of Ingalls Peak's three summits. The standard route ascends the north ridge/gullies from the North-South col to the summit block, where a short, exposed high-Class-3 move on solid rock gains the true summit. Scramble features solid, high-friction Jurassic peridotite throughout. Descent reverses the ascent via the same ridge/gully system. Total round trip approximately 11 miles (17.7 km) and 3,500–4,200 ft of elevation gain.
overview: South Peak (7,640 ft) is the southernmost and easiest of Ingalls Peak's three summits — the taller North Peak (7,662 ft) requires Class 4 climbing and the East Peak is minimum Class 5. All three rise on the same sound, high-friction Jurassic peridotite that makes the Ingalls massif a favorite scrambling/rock destination, immediately west of turquoise Lake Ingalls. The standard South Peak line is an ~11-mile round trip with roughly 3,500–4,200 ft of gain (trailhead figures vary by source): hike to the col between the North and South Peaks, then follow the north ridge/gullies (Class 2-3) to the summit block, where a short, exposed high-Class-3 (locally called low-Class-4) move on solid rock — with an optional squeeze-chimney to dodge the worst exposure — gains the true summit.

current.approach: Park at the Esmeralda (Lake Ingalls) Trailhead at the end of the Teanaway River Road (FS-9737), roughly 4,300 ft, on the edge of the Alpine Lakes Wilderness. Start on Ingalls Way Trail #1390: at about 0.4 mile a junction splits off the Esmeralda Basin Trail (stay right/uphill on Ingalls Way), and at roughly 1.5 miles the Longs Pass Trail #1229 branches right (continue straight, staying on #1390). The trail climbs steadily through open larch and subalpine slopes to Ingalls Pass (~6,500 ft) at about 3 miles, the first point with a clear view of Mount Stuart across the valley. From the pass the trail drops about a mile and several hundred feet into the basin to Lake Ingalls (~6,450 ft), the last reliable water source — carry water from here, as none is available higher. Leave the maintained trail at the lake and pick a way up talus, slabs, and boulders (an obvious dike/gully line is the easiest going) to the notch/col between Ingalls North and South Peaks; aim to pass just left of a small rock spire that sits in the saddle. Steep snow or verglas commonly lingers on the approach to the col into mid-summer, and an ice axe (sometimes crampons) is worth carrying through July. From the col, do not continue straight up the ridge crest — instead drop about 50 ft onto the west side of the ridge and climb one of several Class 2–3 gullies (~100 ft) back up to the crest, then follow the ridge over a mix of snow and blocky rock, with some exposure, to the South Peak summit. Round trip is roughly 11 miles with about 4,200 ft of cumulative gain. The route above the lake is unmarked and involves genuine route-finding on loose talus and boulders — this is the crux of the day for most parties, more so than any single move.
approach_variant_names: Ingalls Way Trail to Lake Ingalls and the North–South col
current.descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: downclimb the ridge and the Class 2–3 gully back down to the North/South col, then pick your way back down the talus, slabs, and any lingering snow to Lake Ingalls, and rejoin Ingalls Way Trail #1390 back over Ingalls Pass to the Esmeralda Trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb scramble — no fixed rappel anchors exist on the standard South Peak route and the great majority of parties downclimb the entire route car-to-car in a day. Watch for loose rock and scree in the gully below the col (parties should stay bunched or descend one at a time to avoid knocking rock onto climbers below), and for the same lingering steep snow/ice near the col noted on the approach, which can make the downclimb more consequential than the ascent, especially early or late season. Some parties in icy conditions choose to sling a natural rock horn or block near the col and back up the short Class 3 step with a hand line or short rappel for extra security, but this is a personal-judgment call, not a standard part of the route, and no such anchor is left in place. The steep dusty climbers' path from the col is slick and a snow patch can linger across it into August; boulders beside it grip better than the dust.
bivy: Beverly and De Roux campgrounds and the North Fork Teanaway roadside camps
current.rope_note: Standard Class 2-3 route via gullies from the notch; Mountaineers guidance recommends an ice axe for snow near the gap and a scramble harness for first-time T3 scramblers, but no rope is used on the standard line.

name: Sean's Route/Second Wind
beta: From below Home Lake the northwest face of Inner Constance comes into view. The route climbs roughly 3 pitches through a crack system over rotten, loose rock to a cave beneath an overhanging roof; the crux is building an anchor there and making an exposed, committing move out of the cave by underclinging the roof and traversing right about 10-15 ft. Several further pitches of class 4-to-low-5th climbing lead to the false summit. Protection is sparse throughout (roughly one usable placement per 20-100 ft).
overview: A 3-pitch alpine trad line up a crack system on Inner Constance's northwest buttress, finished by an exposed roof exit and several pitches of unroped class 4-to-low-5th scrambling to the false summit; a 2021 variation finish on the original 1983 Northwest Buttress line.

current.approach: Hike the Upper Dungeness Trail from the Upper Dungeness trailhead about 9.3 miles uphill to Home Lake and on to a basecamp at the boulders beyond it, from which the route's face is visible from below.
approach_variant_names: Upper Dungeness Trail to Home Lake and the boulder camp — the same start as the Northwest Buttress
current.descent: From the false summit, downclimb exposed, broken ridge terrain, then work down a loose, sandy ledge system into Avalanche Canyon; traverse the canyon back around to the Home Lake cirque to close the loop. The first-ascent party's round trip (climb plus this descent) took about 12.5 hours.
current.detailed_rack: Standard alpine trad rack to a #4 cam, with doubles in the 0.3-0.75 range especially helpful; gear placements are sparse on the rotten rock, averaging roughly one placement per 20-100 ft of climbing.
current.pro_needs: Sparse protection throughout on loose rock — expect long runouts between placements, particularly through the crack system below the roof and on the upper class 4-to-low-5th pitches.

name: Inspiration Traverse
beta: From high camp on the edge of the Inspiration Glacier, the peaks can be taken in any order, but a common plan is Eldorado first (a short climb up the snow of its East Ridge to an exposed, knife-edge snow crest at the summit), then east across the Inspiration Glacier to camp at the rock col on the south side of Klawatti. From there, continue over the Klawatti Glacier and the North Klawatti Glacier to Primus, whose south side is easy snow, slabs and mostly stable talus, reaching the south ridge a short way below the top. Austera, reached from the Klawatti/Austera glacier side, has a snowy ridge between its false and true summits and then a short chimney with 4th-class to low-5th mantle moves; most parties belay it and rappel once. Klawatti is climbed from the col on its south side: cross the moat, climb a steep gully with several 4th-class moves (or two or three short low-5th pitches on the southwest buttress), then scramble loose rock and an easy ridge to the long summit; descend with a rappel back over the moat. Dorado Needle is reached from the McAllister Glacier side: gain the ridge north of the peak, then follow an exposed knife-edge ridge that is crossed au cheval to a tiny summit, where the final move is a short, awkward boulder problem up an angled crack in a steep step (about 5.7-5.9). Descend by rappel rather than re-crossing the knife edge, then return over the Inspiration and Eldorado glaciers to the car.
overview: A glaciated high traverse through the heart of the North Cascades that links five of the range's big summits: Eldorado Peak, Dorado Needle, Klawatti Peak, Austera Peak and Primus Peak. This version starts and ends at the Eldorado Creek trailhead on the Cascade River Road, crossing the Eldorado, Inspiration, McAllister and Klawatti glaciers out to Primus and back. It is serious, committing terrain: crevassed ice, steep snow, moats and short, exposed rock summit blocks, far from any easy exit.

current.approach: From the Eldorado Creek trailhead on the Cascade River Road, walk a short way down the road and cross the Cascade River on a log. A steep climbers' trail then gains roughly 1,800 ft through forest to a large boulder field around 4,000 ft. Cross the boulder field and Eldorado Creek into the open Eldorado Creek basin, climb to a notch on the ridge above, and drop into the Roush Creek basin at the foot of the Eldorado Glacier. Rope up and climb the Eldorado Glacier north to the broad, flat Inspiration Glacier, where the usual high camp sits on rock at the glacier's edge below Eldorado's East Ridge.
current.descent: Reverse the approach: from the Klawatti col camp or the Inspiration Glacier high camp, cross back over the Inspiration Glacier, descend the Eldorado Glacier to the Roush Creek basin, climb back over the notch into the Eldorado Creek basin, then descend the boulder field and the steep forest trail to the Cascade River log crossing and the car. The boulder field and the steep, rooty trail below it are slow and hard on tired legs.
rack: A few small to medium cams
A few nuts
Several slings
Cord or webbing to back up rappel anchors
Pickets for steep snow and crevasse rescue
An ice screw or two for crevasse rescue
current.pro_needs: A light rack is enough for belaying the short 4th and low-5th summit blocks and the Dorado Needle boulder move. Carry spare webbing to back up fixed rappel anchors.
current.rope_note: One glacier rope for the team, also used to belay and rappel the short summit blocks. A 60 m rope covers the single rappels on Austera and Klawatti; a longer rope gives more margin for rappelling Dorado Needle.

name: Internal Combustion
beta: Begins with juggy holds and progresses through increasingly technical movement. The crux comes right before the last bolt, with an option to move right or take a recently-cleaned left-side slot finish. Anchors sit 6 ft above the final bolt, partly hidden behind small trees.
overview: The last route on the Minidike face, a little up the talus; juggy start building to a technical crux near the top.

current.approach: The Dikes sit in the Umatilla National Forest's Walla Walla Ranger District, in the East Fork Touchet River valley near Ski Bluewood, southeast Washington — not near the Snake River. Access is via North Touchet Road out of Dayton, WA, paved for roughly the first 15-16 miles before becoming gravel Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary; the road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter, but snow on the crags and approach slopes keeps the climbing season to roughly May-October, sometimes from April. Approaches are very short and roadside: the south Megadike is reached by parking near a bridge 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and scrambling directly up the steep hillside above the bridge abutment, while Weeping Wall and Joe's Rock are similar short pullout-to-cliff scrambles at 1.1 and 2.0 miles past the same trailhead respectively. The area is lightly visited and faint-trailed, and the basalt is notably loose/fractured, requiring routine loose-rock cleaning. For the Minidike, pull off 1.5 miles beyond the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead, on the left (SE) side of the road immediately after the bridge over the river. Cross the road, scramble down the bridge abutment, and follow a trail downstream on the NW side.
current.descent: Lower from the chain anchor (8 bolts) on a single strand.
current.detailed_rack: 8 bolts to chains, set 6 ft above the final bolt behind small trees.
current.pro_needs: Fully bolted (8 bolts).
current.rope_note: Single-pitch bolted sport route at Minidike (The Dikes, WA). Minidike routes are shorter than Megadike; 60m is sufficient.

name: West Ridge / North Ridge via Chetwoot Lake
beta: A long backcountry approach (6.6+ trail miles, ~3,400 ft gain to Chetwoot Lake) followed by off-trail cross-country travel and unroped class 3 scrambling on the west and north ridges. Solid granite in places but loose talus and scree lower down; most parties treat it as a 2-3 day trip with a camp at Big Heart or Chetwoot Lake.
overview: Iron Cap Mountain (6,347 ft) rises above the Williams Lake and La Bohn Gap country near the heart of the Alpine Lakes Wilderness. Despite its modest elevation, it has striking local relief, climbing about 2,500 feet above the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Valley in less than a mile. The mountain straddles two drainages: its south side sheds into tributaries of the Snoqualmie River via the Williams Lake basin, while the north side drains toward the Foss River. It was first climbed in 1925 by a party led by Seattle mountaineer Joe Hazard. This route comes in from the north on the West Fork Foss River trail off US 2, past Trout, Copper and Big Heart lakes to a camp at Chetwoot Lake, and finishes on Iron Cap's west and north ridges.

current.approach: Start at the West Fork Foss River trailhead (~1,650 ft): from US 2 at Skykomish, turn south on Foss River Road (FR 68), then left on FR 6835 (signed for Trail 1064) for its last 1.9 miles to the trailhead. Self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permits are at the trailhead. The West Fork Foss Lakes Trail #1064 reaches Trout Lake at 1.6 miles, then climbs to Copper Lake (4.2 miles, about 2,400 ft of gain) and continues past Little Heart Lake to Big Heart Lake (7.3 miles, about 3,300 ft), where the maintained trail ends. From Big Heart, go cross-country over the south end of Atrium Ridge, past small tarns and Little Chetwoot Lake, to Chetwoot Lake, the usual camp. From Chetwoot, climb talus and heather toward Point 6077, pass it on the east through more talus, and gain Iron Cap's west ridge for easy Class 3 scrambling. A short third-class downclimb drops into a notch; beyond it a wide ramp traverses below the summit block, without sidehilling, to the broad north ridge, and easy red-tinged rock and dirt lead to the 6,347 ft summit. A variation climbs from the Iron Cap Lake outlet on ledges around the nose of the north ridge. Route-finding through the boulder fields is the crux of the approach: cairns are sparse, and a map or GPS track is strongly advised. Most parties take two to three days, about 24 miles round trip.
approach_variant_names: Iron Cap Lake basin to the north ridge
current.descent: Descent reverses the ascent or loops through the Iron Cap Lake basin. From the summit, follow the broad north ridge down on easy red-tinged rock and dirt, then either return across the ramp and up out of the notch onto the west ridge and down the talus to Chetwoot Lake, or continue down the north ridge to Iron Cap Lake and work back to camp through the lake basin. This is a Class 2-3 walk-off with no fixed anchors or rappels. The main hazards are loose dirt over rock, especially when wet or with snow patches early in the season, and picking the wrong line: parties who lose the ramp or wander east end up cliffed out on the steeper east-side rock bands or in steep heather, so retrace your ascent track. From Chetwoot, reverse the cross-country leg over Atrium Ridge to Big Heart Lake and walk the West Fork Foss trail about 7.3 miles back to the trailhead.
current.pro_needs: No technical protection is needed — this is an unroped class 3 scramble on talus and blocky rock.
current.rope_note: Class 3 scramble on stepped rock terrain (Alpine Lakes Wilderness); no rope standard. Ice axe useful for early-season snow approach via Chetwoot Lake/West Fork Foss.

name: Northwest Ridge / South Face
beta: The easiest way up Ives Peak is a scramble. The standard approach follows the Pacific Crest Trail / Goat Rocks crest, which runs close to the peak's western slopes, then leaves the crest at the col northwest of the peak and follows the northwest ridge and a short south-face scramble to the summit; this is unroped class 2-3 talus/scree, not a technical rock or ice route. The ridge north of the summit is rocky and wind-scoured, with a short loose section near the col, and snow lingers on the peak's flanks into early summer.
overview: Ives Peak (7,920+ ft) is the fourth-highest summit in the Goat Rocks Wilderness, sitting on the main crest between Old Snowy Mountain (7,880+ ft) to the north and Gilbert Peak (Mt. Curtis Gilbert), 8,184 ft, the range high point to the south. The peak straddles the Lewis/Yakima county line and is an eroded remnant of the Goat Rocks volcanic complex, an extinct stratovolcano active from roughly 3.2 million to 500,000 years ago; glaciation and hydrothermal alteration have since stripped away most of its outer flanks, exposing resistant volcanic dikes and spines. A small remnant glacier, the McCall Glacier, clings to Ives' northeast slope and feeds the Tieton River, while the west-facing slopes drain to the Cispus River. There is no maintained trail to the summit and nothing technical is required, but Ives sees only a fraction of the traffic of neighboring Old Snowy Mountain because of the off-trail travel and routefinding involved.

current.approach: Start at the Snowgrass Trailhead (elev. ~4,650 ft), reached via FR-21 (Johnson Creek Road) off US-12 about 3 miles west of Packwood. From the trailhead, follow the Snowgrass Trail #96 south then east through dense forest; the trail drops slightly (~75 ft) to cross Goat Creek on a footbridge/plank crossing around the 2-mile mark (only real water crossing on the approach, and a reliable water source — top off here or at the creeks in upper Snowgrass Flat). Continue climbing through subalpine forest and meadow to Lower Snowgrass Flat, then Upper Snowgrass Flat at roughly 6,400 ft (about 4 miles / ~1,800 ft gain from the trailhead) — a broad, popular wildflower meadow, closed to camping, with multiple small creeks (last dependable water before the ridge). From Upper Snowgrass Flat, continue about 0.3–0.5 mile further to the junction with the Pacific Crest Trail. Follow the PCT north to about 6,700 ft, then leave it and head off-trail to the northeast, ascending talus and scree with no defined tread (occasional cairns) toward the low col on the ridge crest between Old Snowy Mountain and Ives Peak — expect loose, unconsolidated talus that shifts underfoot; test holds and footing carefully. From the col, follow the ridge crest or a line just south of it (Class 2) over a rounded intermediate high point toward Ives' northwest ridge. At the base of the true summit block, a boot path threads up scree toward a notch between two rock outcrops; above the notch is a short cliff band — downclimb slightly and traverse a narrow, exposed ledge (Class 2) to gain the upper south face, then scramble roughly 40 ft to climber's right on loose blocky rock and up easy terrain to the 7,920-ft summit. Snowfields commonly linger on the approach slopes and in the col well into July (this basin can hold 25–40 ft of winter snowpack), so an ice axe is worth carrying for early/mid-season attempts on the traverse. Beyond the pavement the last stretch of the forest road to the trailhead is long, washboarded gravel; a high-clearance car is more comfortable.
approach_variant_names: Snowgrass Trail, the PCT junction and the Old Snowy to Ives col
current.descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: downclimb the loose Class 3 upper south face and the exposed ledge/cliff-band notch back to the northwest ridge, then follow the ridge crest back toward the Old Snowy–Ives col. From the col, most parties either (a) drop directly southwest through the scree/talus basin to regain the PCT — faster but the loosest, choss-iest line, or (b) traverse back over to Old Snowy Mountain and descend its established south-ridge boot path to the PCT near the Packwood Glacier bench, which avoids the worst loose rock directly below Ives' summit block. Either way, once back on the PCT, retrace it south to the Snowgrass Trail #96 junction and follow Snowgrass Trail #96 back down through Upper/Lower Snowgrass Flat and the Goat Creek crossing to the trailhead. This is entirely a scramble walk-off/downclimb — no fixed anchors, bolts, or rope work are involved or needed on this route. Primary descent hazards are the same loose talus/scree encountered on the ascent (higher consequence going downhill) and lingering snow/ice in the col and on the ridge crest into early-mid summer; a short glissade or scree-ski of the basin below the col is a common (optional) shortcut for the descent when snow-free.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rack is used on the standard route; it is an unroped, non-technical scramble.
current.pro_needs: None — the standard route has no fixed protection or belays; consider an ice axe if snow still lingers on the crest or the peak's north/east-facing terrain early in the season.
bivy: Lower Snowgrass Flat / Lily Basin Trail (#86) junction
current.rope_note: Class 2-3 scramble on loose volcanic rock; short exposed ledge traverse (~40ft) below the summit cliff band. Helmet recommended for rockfall on notoriously loose Goat Rocks rock.

name: Jötnar
beta: This is the only repeatable Grade VI big wall in the Pacific Northwest with bolted stainless steel anchors and portaledge bivy opportunities achievable by experienced wall climbers in 3-4 days. Climbing follows a continuous crack system featuring varied aid pitches including thin pins, rivets, hooks, and roof passages. The Fang Roof (Pitch 8) stands out as a classic pitch with hand crack free climbing through an overhang. Plan for 7 days of capsule-style climbing with portaledge camps to complete the first ascent.
overview: Jötnar is the most sustained aid route in Washington State, ascending the left side of Mount Index's North Norwegian Buttress via a continuous crack system located approximately 100 yards left of the Doorish line. The route features 2,000 feet of mixed free and aid climbing across 16 pitches on granite with strong alpine ambiance.

current.approach: From the Lake Serene Trailhead, hike Trail #1068 about 4 miles and 2,000 ft of gain to Lake Serene, then follow the unofficial path around the right-hand (west) side of the lake and traverse talus and huge boulders toward its south end below the Middle Peak (Jötunheim) massif. This cirque holds the Norwegian Buttresses, home to big-wall routes like Jötnar, one of the tallest walls in the Lower 48; reaching the base involves further talus and brush travel beyond the lake. Given the technical, multi-day nature of routes here, most parties approach with overnight gear.
approach_variant_names: Lake Serene talus to the left side of the buttress
current.descent: The descent is accomplished by rappelling the route in full. Due to the sustained overhanging terrain throughout most pitches, careful anchor placement is critical, particularly on pitches with significant roofs. Climbers should plan to use at least two ropes for rappelling. The first ascent team used an unconventional technique where one climber managed haul bags on a very long rappel before the remaining climbers rappelled in pairs off stainless steel anchors. Plan to remove fixed lines during descent to preserve the rock.
current.detailed_rack: Climbers should bring a double rack of nuts and cams ranging from micronuts to #4 Camalots with one #5 Camalot. Include a single set of offset cams, 5 each of beaks in various sizes, 2 lost arrows for aid placement, and 10 rivet hangers (some in #1 size for deeper rivets). Two sets of hooks are essential given the blank sections requiring creative aid placements. The route features bolted anchors, but climbers should verify anchor condition before committing full body weight and be prepared for occasional loose bolts.
rack: Double rack of nuts and cams (micronuts to #4 Camalot, single #5)
Single set of offset cams
Two 60m/70m ropes (lead line + static haul line)
current.pro_needs: Protection is a mix of aid placements and bolted anchors. Lower pitches rely on crack climbing with natural protection (nuts and cams), while upper pitches require rivet placements, hooks, and beaks on blank sections. The route features some bolted anchors already in place from the first ascent, but climbers must assess anchor condition, bring spares for critical bivy sites, and be prepared for creative placements on sections lacking traditional cracks.
bivy: On-wall ledges, Jotunheim and the Norwegian Buttresses
Lake Serene basin and the talus under the Norwegian Buttresses
current.rope_note: Grade VI big wall (16 pitches); climbed with a lead line plus separate static haul line for portaledge/haul bag, and typically two 60m ropes for multi-day rappel descent. All anchors bolted except pitch 15; fixed lines often left on pitch 7.

name: Nohokomeen Glacier and Headwall
beta: This is an early-season snow climb, done when the north cirque is still filled in. From the East Bank Trailhead follow the East Bank Trail roughly 8 miles to the May Creek camp, then leave the trail and climb about 3 miles of steep, bushy, cliff-banded forest — cliff bands start around 3,200 ft and are passed on game trails — to reach snowline near 4,800-5,000 ft and a camp either on the flats around 5,200 ft below the glacier or higher on the glacier itself around 7,400 ft. The Nohokomeen Glacier runs from about 6,100 ft to 8,200 ft, is over 340 acres, and is heavily crevassed after the midpoint of its descent, so rope up. Above the glacier the headwall is the crux: it is variously described as 700 vertical feet of snow at slopes up to 60 degrees, and as a sustained 50-55 degrees for about 800 feet with steeper steps. Most parties simul-climb it, taking turns kicking steps, with a rope over the shoulder for the bergschrund; winter parties have pitched it out with pickets, cams, nuts and screws through a mixed cliff band. The bergschrund is the main obstacle and normally goes on a single bridge on the left side. Above, exit onto the ridge and finish along a narrow, corniced summit ridge with rocky drops — the last few hundred feet are the most exposed of the route.
overview: The classic north-side snow route on Jack Mountain and by far the best documented line on the peak: the East Bank Trail to May Creek, a steep bushwhack to the Nohokomeen Glacier, then roughly 2,100 ft of crevassed glacier and a 700-800 ft headwall of sustained 50-60 degree snow to a corniced summit ridge. The round trip is rated at 30 miles and 10,000 ft of gain and graded an intermediate alpine climb.

current.approach: From SR 20 milepost 138, park at the East Bank Trailhead (~1,800 ft) and descend briefly to the bridge over Ruby Creek. Follow the East Bank Trail — mostly flat and fast — roughly 8 miles north along Ross Lake to the May Creek camp. (Ross Lake Resort's water taxi will drop parties on the eastern shore and is a legitimate way to skip most of the trail; check current rates and schedule directly with the resort.) At May Creek leave the trail and climb steeply east, loosely ascending between the creeks on the west side of Jack Mountain. Cliff bands begin around 3,200 ft and are threaded on boot and game trails; snow generally appears around 4,800-5,000 ft. About 3 miles of this off-trail work reaches a flat camp just over 5,200 ft below the glacier toe. Strong parties push a second camp onto the upper glacier around 7,400 ft, which shortens summit day considerably. Before the highway opens, parties have biked about 4 miles from the MP 134 gate to the trailhead and continued on foot or ski.
approach_variant_names: East Bank Trail on foot from milepost 138, leaving it at May Creek
Water taxi up Ross Lake to the eastern shore, cutting out most of the trail
Before the highway opens: the gate at milepost 134
current.descent: There is no rappel line — the standard descent is to downclimb what you climbed, ideally in your own steps. Reverse the corniced summit ridge carefully, then face-in downclimb the headwall; parties that are not comfortable simul-downclimbing 50-60 degree snow lower each other off buried pickets on the steepest 100 m or so. Recross the bergschrund at the same bridge you used on the way up, and be aware that it will be softer and less trustworthy than it was in the morning. Descend the glacier roped, aiming to be off the snow before it crusts up or, in spring, before afternoon warming makes the lower slopes unstable. From the glacier toe, retrace the bushwhack down through the cliff bands to camp — this is genuinely hard to navigate in the dark and several parties have relied on GPS to find their line back through the timber. Reported summit-to-camp times run from about 2.5 hours (fast, in good steps) to considerably longer. From camp it is the 3-mile descent to May Creek and 8 miles of flat trail back to the car.
current.detailed_rack: A snow rack, not a rock rack. Carry a 60 m rope per rope team, harnesses, a full crevasse-rescue kit (prusiks, pulley, three or four locking carabiners), and three to four snow pickets — pickets are the workhorse here, used for the bergschrund, for running belays on the headwall and for lowering on the descent. Two ice screws are worth carrying for the years when the headwall turns out to be ice rather than neve. On the winter ascent through the cliff band, teams carried cams, nuts, hexes and screws.
current.pro_needs: Pickets for snow, screws as a backup for ice, and a rock anchor or two only if the headwall's cliff band is melted out and you must climb mixed ground. In good May conditions most parties place almost nothing and simul-climb the headwall, so protection is more about having a retreat plan than about protecting the leader.
bivy: High camp below the Nohokomeen Glacier

name: Northeast Glacier
beta: From the upper basin east of Jack, climb moraine and snow to the serrated rock col just east of the Southeast Ridge. Cross a little west of its lowest point; elsewhere the far side is too steep. Downclimb roughly 250 ft of broken rock and snow gullies onto the glacier, then traverse to its narrow northern part and find a way through. The glacier is chaotic and usually only goes in early summer. The first party had to leave it for snow and rock on the buttress to its right, then traversed back across the ice to the notch below the summit. From the notch, finish as for the North Ridge. Allow about six hours from camp.
overview: A seldom-climbed glacier line on Jack's northeast side. From the basin east of the mountain you cross a jagged rock col east of the Southeast Ridge, drop onto a small, chaotic glacier, and work up its narrow northern part, using the buttress on its right where the ice is too broken, to the notch below the summit. The last stretch follows the North Ridge to the top.

current.approach: From the Canyon Creek Trailhead on SR 20 near milepost 141 (about 1,900 ft), ford Canyon Creek - there is no bridge, and the creek runs high and hazardous into midsummer - and climb the switchbacks of Jackita Ridge Trail #738 to the Crater Lake junction. Continue up the Crater Mountain trail to about 6,700 ft, then leave it on a rising traverse to the pass near 7,000 ft between Crater Mountain's main summit and its east summit. Descend steep snow and the crevassed Jerry Glacier toward Jerry Lakes and work around to a camp near 6,000 ft on the east side of Jack. From camp, climb to the serrated rock col east of the Southeast Ridge and drop about 250 ft on its far side onto the Northeast Glacier. There is no boot track or cairn beyond Crater Lake.
approach_variant_names: Canyon Creek Trailhead, Crater Lake, and the pass between Crater Mountain's summits
current.descent: There is no published descent for this route. The realistic options are to reverse the glacier — which on steep, heavily crevassed ice means downclimbing and/or lowering with pickets and screws, and re-crossing the bergschrund — or to traverse to the East Ridge or North Ridge and descend that, both of which are Grade II Class 4 and were used as a descent line by at least one party (a 2006 party ascended the North Ridge and descended the East Ridge). Descending the South Face toward Jerry Lakes is a third option, but it leaves you working back around the mountain to a camp on its east side. Whichever you choose, scout it before you climb; committing to an unknown descent on Jack's loose rock in fading light is how this mountain generates epics.
current.detailed_rack: Standard glacier travel kit — rope and pickets — for the steep, heavily crevassed glacier, plus a light rock rack for the class 4 rock near the summit ridge.
current.pro_needs: Snow and ice protection dominates: pickets for neve, screws where the glacier is hard, and running belays for crevasse-riddled terrain. Rock protection is limited to whatever the loose greenstone summit block offers.
bivy: Camp on the east side of Jack

beta: Bolts to anchors. Real short route, great for teaching new climbers.
overview: Short sport climb suitable for teaching new climbers, though somewhat difficult to access.

name: Northeast Buttress
beta: Modern parties climbing the fuller/harder version of the same buttress rate it Grade V, 5.8, AI2: a short approach leads to loose lower slabs, then thousands of feet of near-vertical vegetation (alder, turf, heather), a 5.5-5.8 rock band to a ~7,100 ft bivy, an exposed snow arête, and a short ice pitch to the summit ridge.
overview: Johannesburg Mountain's Northeast Buttress is one of the great long alpine routes of the North Cascades: a sustained, roughly twenty-pitch line up the same immense northeast face that drops nearly 5,000 ft in under a mile above the Cascade Pass road. It's rated no harder than 5.8 technically, but carries an outsized reputation among North Cascades climbers — less for pure difficulty than for its relentless length and complex, mixed terrain, including stretches of steep heather and brush low on the route that regulars describe as 'vertical bushwhacking' or 'tree climbing.' Most parties bivy partway up, commonly around 7,100 ft below the final headwall, and the route has a long history of climbers returning a day or two later than planned.

current.approach: Start at the Cascade Pass Trailhead (~3,600 ft) at the end of Cascade River Road. Rather than taking the maintained Cascade Pass Trail, leave the trail near the parking lot/hairpin area and descend a dirt/brush embankment down to the Cascade River, then ford it — this is a cold, glacial-melt crossing that runs highest in the afternoon on hot days, so an early start (or crossing on the return before flows peak) is worth planning for. From the river, climb up and over the debris/terminal moraine below the peak's northeast face and pick up a boot path. At roughly 3,500 ft you'll reach an obvious snow finger/couloir; follow it up and climber's-right onto the toe of the Northeast Buttress (Rib). Above the snow finger there is no trail — the route is sustained, steep vegetable-and-rock climbing: hand-over-hand up alder in a mossy streambed, steep turf and heather, and short stretches of tunneling through subalpine trees, trending right to gain the buttress/rib crest around 5,000–5,500 ft. From the crest, steep heather slopes lead into 4th-class rock, and the crest is followed (with a few pitches of low 5th class in spots) up to a snow arête that runs nearly to the summit snowfield; parties often bivy around 7,100 ft. In under a mile of horizontal distance you gain roughly 3,500–4,600 ft, so this is one of the steeper, more sustained approaches in the Cascades — expect route-finding through the brush/heather bands, loose rock and moraine underfoot low down, and real rockfall exposure in the snow-finger/couloir section if other parties are above. Water is available at the river ford and from seasonal seeps/snow lower on the buttress, but there is none once you're up on rock.
approach_variant_names: Cascade Pass trailhead, river ford and the snow finger
current.descent: Descend via the long East Ridge, not a walk-off — it is a sustained, loose, exposed ridge traverse in its own right. From the summit, work east along the ridge, connecting loose 3rd/4th-class ledges roughly 75 ft below the actual crest to bypass a series of gendarmes. As the ridge steepens into more of a buttress dropping toward the C-J col (the saddle between Johannesburg and Cascade Peak), you have two options: rappel a series of anchors along the crest, or downclimb a loose gully just to climber's right of the rap line. Most parties rappel this section — parties describe on the order of 6–8 raps to reach the col (one recent party made two full 60m raps in a gully with natural rock anchors partway and atop the gully; another describes roughly 7 shorter raps off slings/tat on the crest), so bring a 60m rope and a small rack of slings/cord for building or backing up anchors — these are natural anchors (horns, blocks, sometimes fixed webbing) rather than bolted stations, and existing tat should be inspected before trusting it. From the C-J col, the standard descent (locally called "Doug's Direct") traverses beneath the Triplets buttress, sidehills across steep meadows, climbs to the north ridge of Mixup Peak, drops via 3rd/4th-class slabs and blocks to the Cache Glacier, then follows a climber's trail along Mixup Arm back down toward the Cascade Pass Trail and the road — roughly 5 hours from the col to the car. Watch for loose rock throughout the ridge and gully sections, and for the same cold Cascade River ford on the final approach back to the trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: A single to double rack of cams from 0.4 to 3 inches, a set of nuts, about 10 alpine draws with doubles, and two ropes for rappels.
current.pro_needs: The rock pitches protect reasonably on the better stone, but much of the route is moderate, run-out, or mixed terrain where speed and judgment matter more than gear. Snow and ice sections take occasional pickets or screws.
bivy: Buttress bivy at the heather-to-rock transition
Chopped platforms on the upper glacier
